Good morning.

Anti-Jewish discrimination and legitimate criticism of Israeli state actions became conflated into one offence by Italy’s parliament on Tuesday (17 November).

Adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) official definition of anti-semitism, Rome’s bill will apply across schools, universities, social-media platforms, and beyond. The move has raised serious concerns about what this will do to freedom of expression and protest.

Despite not imposing financial penalties or criminal sanctions for offenders, it shows which side of history far-right prime minister Georgia Meloni’s Italy has chosen...

NEWSLETTER · 20 Nov 2026, 07:05

Schwesig: Die Frau, die sich bestimmt bald traut

Präsentiert von Die L’Oréal Gruppe Von RASMUS BUCHSTEINER Mit FERDINAND KNAPP PRÄSENTIERT VON Schicken Sie uns Ihre Tipps hier oder hier | X @vonderbu

Präsentiert von Die L’Oréal Gruppe

Von RASMUS BUCHSTEINER

Mit FERDINAND KNAPP

PRÄSENTIERT VON

Schicken Sie uns Ihre Tipps hier oder hier | X @vonderburchard @R_Buchsteiner | Das Playbook anhören oder online lesen

Guten Morgen! Hier meldet sich Rasmus Buchsteiner direkt aus dem Regierungsviertel. Für mich geht es gleich in die Leipziger Straße, in den Bundesrat — wegen Hendrik Wüst. Und, klar, auch wegen Manuela Schwesig.

Machtreserven: Die Länderkammer ist ein Panoptikum derer, die mal wichtiger werden könnten. Wüst spricht dort erstmals als Präsident des Bundesrats. Schwesig gilt als Frau, die sich bestimmt bald traut: SPD-Chefin zu werden.

Sonst bei uns: Die wichtigsten Takeaways des Ukraine-Gipfels im Kanzleramt, die Agenda im Bundesrat, die große Personalfrage bei den Freien Wählern und Merz’ Weihnachtsbaum.

Besondere Empfehlung: Am Samstag hören Sie Gordons Spaziergang mit der eigentlich gewählten Präsidentin von Belarus, Swetlana Tichanowskaja. Im Security Sunday spricht Rixa Fürsen mit Robert Habeck darüber, warum der Blick in die Arktis zeigt, wie sich globale Machtverhältnisse verschieben könnten.

**(Anzeige) Eine Nachricht der L’Oréal Gruppe: Für die L’Oréal Gruppe ist Deutschland langfristig ein strategischer Produktionsstandort von globaler Bedeutung. Mehr erfahren**

SEITE EINS

DRAUSSEN VOR DER TÜR: Es war kalt. Es war nicht trocken. Zum Glück hatte ich einen dieser schönen roten Regenschirme dabei, auf dem in weißen Buchstaben POLITICO steht. Drinnen in der Hamburger Landesvertretung brannte gestern länger Licht.

Spotted: Manuela Schwesig. Sie kam übrigens pünktlich um 18:30 Uhr zum Vor-Bundesrats-Abendessen der SPD, bei dem es diesmal in erweiterter Runde auch um die Neuaufstellung der Partei gehen sollte.

Kurzer O-Ton: Sie freue sich über das Wiedersehen mit ihren MP-Kollegen: „Wir wollen den Bundesrat vorbereiten. Vielen Dank!”

Könnte sein, dass Schwesig heute in der Länderkammer an der Leipziger Straße anders als sonst an den Kameras vorbeigeht. Oder gleich den Hintereingang nimmt.

Denn: Vorerst will sie sich nicht in die Karten blicken lassen. Sie sondiert. Klar bekommt sie mit, dass alles in der Partei auf sie wartet. Und doch will sie sich noch nicht festlegen — auch wenn der Druck steigt.

Beispiel: Diese Woche hier in diesem Interview auf den Stufen der Schweriner Staatskanzlei. Wieder einmal läuft alles und immer wieder auf die eine Frage hinaus: Traut sie sich?

Moment mal: Streng genommen war Schwesig ja schon mal SPD-Chefin — 2019, nach dem Rücktritt von Andrea Nahles. Die Aufgabe, die älteste Partei Deutschlands vorübergehend zu führen, teilte sie sich damals mit Malu Dreyer und Thorsten Schäfer-Gümbel.

Der Eindruck: Lange wird Schwesig nicht mehr allein auf ihre Aufgaben in MV verweisen können. Und darauf, dass sie noch schnell zu Bürgerdialog, Schulbesuch oder Heringsessen muss, in Kandelin, Güstrow oder Wismar.

Nächste Woche ist Schwesig schon wieder in Berlin. Im Willy-Brandt-Haus sogar. Da verleiht sie den Regine-Hildebrandt-Preis. Gelegenheit für das ein oder andere Gespräch am Rande.

Was nun? In der Abwägung aller Argumente gibt es einen für Schwesig sehr gewichtigen Punkt. Sie wäre zwar außerhalb der Berliner Kabinettsdisziplin. Aber als SPD-Chefin wäre sie im Koalitionsausschuss dabei und könnte die Dinge nicht mehr einfach so von der Seitenlinie kommentieren.

Stimmt: So eine Nummer wie im Sommer mit der Rente mit 63, als sie deren Aus infrage stellte, wäre dann nicht mehr möglich.

Das Manko: Sollte Schwesig es bis zur Kanzlerkandidatin bringen, könnte sie im Wahlkampf nur schwer behaupten, sie habe mit der Merz-Regierung nichts zu tun gehabt.

Trivial ist diese Entscheidung auch aus anderen Gründen nicht. Zu berücksichtigen wäre auch, dass nicht alle, die in der Vergangenheit ihr MP-Amt mit dem SPD-Vorsitz kombinieren wollten, dabei glücklich geworden sind. Schwesig könnte ja mal Kurt Beck fragen. Oder vielleicht Matthias Platzeck.

Außergewöhnlich: Die Zurückhaltung der beiden möglichen Männer an der Seite Schwesigs.

Der eine: Hubertus Heil. Er hat ein gutes Verhältnis zu Schwesig. Er vermeidet aber alles, was sie als Vereinnahmung verstehen könnte — besonders in diesem Interview.

Fleißig, fleißig: Ansonsten kämpft Heil wacker. Er sammelt Endorsements — von Abgeordneten und von Parteigliederungen. Gestern kam eins von der SPD-Dortmund vor dem Auftritt des Kandidaten bei der Ruhr-SPD in Essen.

Und der Vizekanzler? Er stapfte gestern um 18:22 Uhr in die Hamburger Landesvertretung, kurz vor Schwesig also.

Routiniert: Lars Klingbeil spult sein Regierungsprogramm ab. Jetzt will er eine Dialogtour durch die Partei machen, auch wenn er öffentlich gesagt hat, dass er nicht an seinem SPD-Chef-Stuhl klebe. Und die Rückmeldungen aus den Landesverbänden sind für ihn auch alles andere als ermutigend.

Doch ein bisschen Pattex: An seinem Chefsessel in der Wilhelmstraße 97 scheint Klingbeil schon zu kleben. Nicht ausgeschlossen, dass er um den Finanzminister-Job kämpfen muss. Auffällig ist, dass er gerade jetzt einen Prozess anstößt, der über den Tag hinaus reicht.

Heute an morgen denken: „Deutschland 2035: Perspektiven für ein starkes Land”, heißt die Überschrift. Beamte, Forscher und Thinktank-Leute sollen bis 2028 möglichst konkrete Vorschläge erarbeiten. Ziel ist ein sogenanntes Weißbuch.

Klingt schon, als habe da jemand noch viel vor. Am 2. Dezember zum Auftakt will Klingbeil eine Grundsatzrede halten. So wie im Frühjahr bei der Bertelsmann-Stiftung.

Kleines Ablenkungsmanöver: Hört man sich in der Union um, dauert es nicht lange, bis die Behauptung kommt, die Krise der Koalition habe eine Menge mit der ungeklärten Führungsfrage in der SPD zu tun.

Andererseits: Mit Schwesig als Parteichefin, deren Verhältnis zu Merz ist, wie es ist, würde der Beziehungsstatus von Union und SPD zusätzlich kompliziert …

DIPLOMATISCHE DEPESCHE

GESTERN WIRKT NACH: Zunächst überraschte Donald Trump die „Koalition der Willigen“ mit einem Anruf aus der Air Force One. Noch mehr überraschte er mit seiner Aussage, dass Putin angeblich Frieden wolle und man statt neuer Ukraine-Hilfen die Milliarden besser anders ausgeben könne/solle, berichten Hans von der Burchard und Tim Ross.

Auch bei den Sicherheitsgarantien bleiben viele offene Fragen: So sagte Jared Kushner, die USA hätten „die Russen davon überzeugt, dass jede Sicherheitsgarantie für die Ukraine auf Artikel 5 beruhen würde.“

Ach ja? Wolodymyr Selenskyj bemerkte daraufhin, er sei sich „nicht sicher“, ob alle Seiten Artikel 5 genauso auslegten „wie wir“. Seien die USA bereit, eigene Militärbasen zur Absicherung in der Ukraine zu eröffnen? Seien sie auch bereit, mit eigenen Soldaten die Ukraine im Falle eines erneuten russischen Angriffs zu verteidigen?

Denn er sei sich sicher: „Sie werden versuchen, es wieder zu tun.“ Der ganze Bericht von Hans hier bei Welt.

Was für Merz bleibt: Der gut besuchte Ukraine-Gipfel im Kanzleramt war ein diplomatischer Erfolg. „Das Treffen in Shenzhen war offenbar vor allem ein Bildtermin“, so der Kanzler. „Hier in Berlin, in der Mitte Europas, formulieren wir gemeinsam, wo wir stehen.“

Anzeige

KANZLERMAPPE

ES GEHT WEITER UM DIE UKRAINE: Am Vormittag nehmen Merz und Reiche am deutsch-ukrainischen Wirtschaftsforum im Haus der Wirtschaft teil. Um 10:20 Uhr spricht der Kanzler.

STAATSBESUCH: Am Nachmittag um 14 Uhr empfängt Merz Scheich Tamim bin Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani – den Emir von Katar also.

WORAUF MERZ AM SAMSTAG SCHAUT: Den neuen Verhandlungsvorschlag für den EU-Haushalt, den António Costa dann präsentieren will. Wie Gregorio Sorgi berichtet, erwägt der EU-Ratspräsident dabei eine EU-Steuer auf US-Digitalunternehmen wie Google und Meta. Für Merz ein sensibles Thema — wegen der Sorge vor neuen Strafzöllen durch Trump.

KANZLER HÄLT VERSPRECHEN: Am Sonntag musiziert Merz um 11:30 Uhr mit Kindern in der SAT.1-Sendung „Frag mal den Kanzler – Kinder treffen Friedrich Merz“. Das geht auf ein Versprechen in einer Wahlsendung während des Wahlkampfs 2025 zurück.

Übrigens: Der Kanzler ist durchaus musikalisch – hier, hier und hier können Sie sich selbst überzeugen.

Blick in die neue Woche: Merz geht Montag zur Fraktionssitzung der Union, Dienstag schaut er sicher im Bundestag vorbei, wenn Klingbeil den Haushaltsentwurf einbringt. Mittwoch ist Generaldebatte mit Kanzler-Auftritt. Und den Parlamentskreis Mittelstand (PKM) trifft er auch.

Wie schön sind Deine Blätter: Am Mittwoch wird der Weihnachtsbaum vor dem Kanzleramt übergeben. Eine Weißtanne soll es sein. Ich höre, diesmal kommt der Baum nicht aus dem Sauerland. Vielleicht hat ja Markus Söder etwas damit zu tun …

LÄNDERPUNKTE

DAS VORLETZTE MAL in diesem Jahr trifft sich heute der Bundesrat. Um das SPD-Kamintreffen in der Hamburger Landesvertretung ging es ja oben schon. Die B-Seite kam übrigens um die Ecke in der Landesvertretung von Thüringen zusammen.

Premiere feiert heute Hendrik Wüst als Bundesratspräsident, also als Nr. 4 in der protokollarischen Rangfolge. Demnächst — wahrscheinlich noch in diesem Jahr — dürfte es auf die erste Auslandsreise in dieser Funktion gehen.

To be spotted: Nina Warken. Die Kanzleramtschefin antwortet heute am Pult im Bundesrat auf Wüsts Antrittsrede. Dürfte alles recht freundlich werden.

Die Tagesordnung: Heute geht es in der Länderkammer unter anderem um 21 Gesetze aus dem Bundesrat und 20 eigene Initiativen.

Zum Beispiel: Um die Notfallreform. Hier gab es zwischen den B-Ländern und dem Bund gestern Abend eine Verständigung. Somit könnte die Reform heute den Bundesrat passieren.

Die Details zur Protokollerklärung, die gestern von der Bundesregierung vorgelegt wurde, lesen Sie in unserem Pro Newsletter Gesundheit.

Anders bei den Kitas: Die Länder sind mit dem Finanzierungsvorschlag des Bundes für Karin Priens Startchancen- und Qualitätsentwicklungsgesetz weiter nicht einverstanden, hört Maximilian Stascheit. Es geht aller Voraussicht nach in den Vermittlungsausschuss.

Heikel, heikel: Heute wird es auch bei zwei Verkehrs-Prestigeprojekten von Steffen Bilger spannend. Bei seinem Autobahn-Kredit befürchten die Länder Mindereinnahmen durch die Umsatzsteuer. Zwar kann der Bundesrat hier nur Stellung nehmen, doch die Länder haben ihre Bedenken längst bei den gerade verhandelnden Bundestagsfraktionen (insbesondere bei der SPD) platziert, erfuhr Cedric Looks.

Der erste Teil der Führerscheinreform wird heute verabschiedet: Doch die für die Reform zentrale Verordnung wurde von der Tagesordnung genommen. Im Gespräch ist, Bilgers günstigeren Führerschein auf Juli 2027 zu schieben.

PARTEIEN

SCHWERES ERBE: Die Freien Wähler beraten am Samstag, Sonntag und Montag über die Nachfolge ihres verstorbenen Parteichefs Hubert Aiwanger, der morgen beigesetzt wird. Wer sich trifft und worüber genau gesprochen wird, ist nicht bekannt.

Als mögliche Nachfolger kursieren die Namen von Bayerns Digitalminister Fabian Mehring und der Regensburger Landrätin Tanja Schweiger, Aiwangers Lebensgefährtin.

Glaskugel: Dass die Partei ihren neuen Bundesvorsitzenden wieder im Freistaat sucht, gilt als wahrscheinlich: Dort lebt die Hälfte ihrer Mitglieder. Allerdings hätte im Bundesvorstand der eine oder andere auch gerne mal einen Kandidaten aus einem anderen Bundesland gesehen.

Drei Ämter, drei Personen? Bald soll auch über Aiwangers Nachfolger als Vize-Ministerpräsident und Wirtschaftsminister abgestimmt werden — die FW brauchen ein oder zwei Kandidaten. Unwahrscheinlich, dass alle drei Ämter — Vize-Ministerpräsident, Wirtschaftsminister und FW-Chef — an ein und dieselbe Person fallen.

PROTESTTAG, DER ZWEITE: Nach den „Gen-Z-regelt“-Demos am 31. Oktober wollen heute erneut junge Menschen auf die Straße gehen. Aufgerufen dazu hat die Bundesschülerkonferenz, die sich von „Gen Z regelt“ distanziert hatte.

Etwas unübersichtlich: Trotzdem haben sich zahlreiche Verbände und Initiativen dem heutigen Protesttag angeschlossen — teils mit anderen Schwerpunkten (Wehrpflicht, Klima, Lebenskosten), teils sogar mit Parallelveranstaltungen.

Hauptsache mitmachen: Die Grüne Jugend hat sowohl an Halloween als auch heute zur Unterstützung der Proteste aufgerufen. Bundessprecher Luis Bobga rechnet sogar mit mehr Teilnehmern als beim letzten Mal.

O-Ton: „Ich kann mir gut vorstellen, dass heute noch mehr junge Menschen auf die Straßen gehen werden, weil die letzten Bilder ja auch gezeigt haben, die Demonstration an sich, die sind friedlich verlaufen“, sagt er im Berlin Playbook Podcast.

Keine Garantie: Erneute Ausschreitungen bei den Protesten könne man „per se nicht verhindern“, so Bobga.

PLENARSAALEBENE

FRÜHAUFSTEHER: Der Haushaltsausschuss trifft sich kommenden Mittwoch von 7:30 Uhr bis 8:45 Uhr zu einer Sondersitzung, um die Ergebnisse des Koalitionsausschusses in den Haushaltsentwurf einzuarbeiten, erfuhr Maximilian. Die finale Debatte im Plenum findet am Freitag ab 12:30 Uhr statt.

LÄNDERPUNKTE

VORVERLEGT: Am 8. Dezember will sich Ulrich Siegmund zum Ministerpräsidenten von Sachsen-Anhalt wählen lassen — doch nicht wie ursprünglich geplant am 15. Dezember. Dafür gibt es zwei Gründe.

Unter Zeitdruck: „Ich brauche Rechtssicherheit für die Kündigung des Medienstaatsvertrages,“ sagte Siegmund der Jungen Freiheit. Umso früher die AfD in die Regierung kommt, desto mehr Zeit hat sie, die Verträge mit ARD, ZDF und Deutschlandradio fristgerecht zu beenden.

Sicher ist sicher: Außerdem plant Siegmund, im ersten Wahlgang gewählt zu werden — doch für den Fall, dass er in den ersten beiden Wahlgängen scheitert, kann es nicht sofort einen dritten geben. Dann müsste man mit dem ursprünglichen Termin bis nach Weihnachten warten.

Das Kalkül: Mit der vorgezogenen Wahl könnte es am 15. Dezember schon einen dritten Wahlgang geben — mit einer einfachen Mehrheit und wie versprochen noch in diesem Jahr.

Nur ein Backup: Denn Siegmund geht davon aus, die fehlenden drei Stimmen für eine erfolgreiche Wahl im ersten Wahlgang bereits organisiert zu haben, wie er der Jungen Freiheit sagte.

EUROVISION

„WOHLSTAND WIRD SOFORT SINKEN“: Der Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) der EU ist der Türkei ein Dorn im Auge. Gestern war der türkische Handelsminister in Berlin, um dafür zu werben, bei „Made in EU“ mitmachen zu dürfen. Auch das deutsche Wirtschaftsmodell sei in Gefahr, sagte er im Interview mit Tom Schmidtgen.

Wenn wir Freunde wären: Der IAA würde türkische Produkte von der Beschaffung und der öffentlichen Förderung ausschließen. Deutschland setzt sich gemeinsam mit Frankreich dafür ein, dass bei Autos nur Produkte aus der EU und Großbritannien als „Made in EU“ gelten. Die Türkei wäre raus.

Das Problem: Die Türkei ist ein wichtiger Teil der Liefer- und Produktionskette der hiesigen Autoindustrie. Dort bauen unter anderem Ford, Renault und Stellantis ihre Autos für den EU-Markt zusammen. Da fast jedes E-Auto subventioniert ist, wäre die gesamte Branche betroffen.

Drohen will er der EU nicht: „Wir werden unsere Rechte natürlich verteidigen, ganz sicher“, sagte Bolat zu Tom. „Aber die Türkei bedient sich niemals der Sprache der Drohungen.“

Wie viele Jobs der Minister für Deutschland in Gefahr sieht, lesen Sie bei Industrie & Handel.

EU-GROSSBRITANNIEN-GIPFEL: In Brüssel treffen sich heute Vertreter der EU und Großbritanniens und sprechen über eine weitere schrittweise Annäherung des Vereinigten Königreichs an die EU.

Es steht viel auf dem Spiel: Für Burnham ist der Gipfel besonders wichtig. Nur wenn er ein Erfolg wird, kann er die Kritiker von einer Annäherung an die EU überzeugen. Was besprochen werden soll, lesen Sie im Newsletter Brussels Decoded und hier.

BENDLERBLOCK

SCHULTERSCHLUSS IN WARSCHAU: Verteidigungsminister Boris Pistorius beendet heute seinen zweitägigen Polen-Besuch mit Kranzniederlegungen in Warschau. Gestern besuchte er die Gedenkstätte Auschwitz-Birkenau und traf seinen Amtskollegen Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz zu Gesprächen.

Schulterschluss: In einem Namensartikel schreiben beide Minister: „Wir wollen den europäischen Pfeiler der NATO stärken und gleichzeitig unser enges transatlantisches Verhältnis bewahren.“

Washington im Blick: „Wir arbeiten eng mit dem Pentagon zusammen“, betonen beide Minister. Eine zentrale Rolle spielt dabei eine von US-Verteidigungsstaatssekretär Elbridge Colby gegründete Gesprächsrunde, in der Washington mit ausgewählten NATO-Staaten darüber berät, wie Europa mehr Verantwortung für seine Verteidigung übernimmt.

JOBWECHSEL

AUFGESTIEGEN: Der Stern-Reporter Julius Betschka wird Chefreporter im Hauptstadtbüro. Dort soll er sich weiter um den Kanzler, die Union und das Innenministerium kümmern. Glückwunsch!

SPOTTED

RELEASE DAY: Zur Veröffentlichung des Gangster-Videospiels GTA 6 stellten zahlreiche Internet-Nutzer KI-generierte Fotos von sich im Stil eines GTA-Posters ins Netz. Auch Politiker und Parteien konnten es nicht lassen — wie etwa Ulrich Siegmund oder die CDU, die den Kanzler im GTA-Stil auf Instagram postete — und sogleich viel Spott erntete, unter anderem von der FDP und den Grünen.

Nicht nur Politiker, sondern auch ihre Ministerien sprangen auf den Hype auf — naja.

AGENDA

— Scheich zu Besuch: Um 10 Uhr empfängt Frank-Walter Steinmeier den Emir von Katar, Scheich Tamim bin Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, mit militärischen Ehren in der Villa Borsig. Um 19:30 Uhr findet ein Staatsbankett im Amtssitz am Spreebogen statt.

— Die Regierungspressekonferenz findet um 11:30 Uhr mit Sebastian Hille statt.

— Antarktis-Expedition: Die Reise von Dorothee Bär endet heute. Gestern hatte sie den Kanzler aus der Arktis per Videocall angerufen, in Begleitung des Astronauten Alexander Gerst.

— Verteidigungsminister in Polen: Heute endet die zweitägige Reise von Boris Pistorius nach Krakau und Warschau.

— Vorlesestunde: Im Rahmen des bundesweiten Vorlesetags besucht Alois Rainer um 8:15 Uhr die Grundschule Ittling in Straubing.

— Weltmeister erklärt Finanzen: An der Auftaktveranstaltung in der Berliner Otto-Hahn-Schule zur Finanzbildungsstrategie nimmt um 9 Uhr Lars Klingbeil mit dem gestern vorgestellten Finanzbildungsbotschafter Philipp Lahm teil.

— Männer im Fokus: Bei der Internationalen Jungen- und Männerkonferenz im Umweltforum Berlin hält Karin Prien um 9 Uhr eine Begrüßungsrede und nimmt anschließend an einem Panel teil.

— Bundespressekonferenz: Um 10 Uhr präsentieren Amy Kirchhoff, Generalsekretärin der Bundesschülerkonferenz, Doreen Siebernik, Vize-Vorsitzende der Gewerkschaft Erziehung und Wissenschaft, Normen Heise, Vorsitzender des Bundeselternrats, und Yasin Hinz, Sprecher von Fridays for Future, ihre Forderungen zum heutigen Bildungsprotest.

— Nordlichter in der Hauptstadt: Um 13 Uhr nimmt Steffen Bilger an der Konferenz Norddeutscher Länder in der Landesvertretung Schleswig-Holstein teil.

— Wirtschaftsministerin in Bayern: Um 18:10 Uhr gibt Katherina Reiche einen Impuls bei der Veranstaltungsreihe „Menschen in Europa“ in Passau und nimmt an einer Podiumsdiskussion teil.

ZU GUTER LETZT

DER WINTER NAHT: Heute kommt am Nachmittag bei kühlen 5 °C die Sonne heraus. Am Wochenende kann es regnen, bei Höchsttemperaturen von 7 °C am Samstag und 6 °C am Sonntag. Nächste Woche wird es dann richtig kalt.

GRUß AUS DER KÜCHE:

— Mitarbeiterrestaurant JKH: Drei Kartoffel-Frischkäsetaschen mit Rahmspinat und Möhren-Rohkostsalat oder Ruppiner Schweinegulasch mit Apfel-Rotkohl und Kartoffelklößen

— Lampenladen PLH: Seelachs in Vollkorn mit Remoulade, dazu Pommes frites und Salatbukett oder Kartoffel-Sauerkraut-Apfel-Puffer, dazu Kräuterquark und Beilagensalat

— Die Kantine RTG hat heute geschlossen.

GEBURTSTAGE: Hennis Herbst, Linken-Landes- und Fraktionsvorsitzender in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (30), Steffen Meyer, stellvertretender Regierungssprecher (41), Katrin Albsteiger, stellvertretende CSU-Vorsitzende (43), Gereon Bollmann, AfD-MdB (73)

Samstag: Philip Hoffmann, CDU-MdB (38), Sebastian Lechner, CDU-Landes- und Fraktionsvorsitzender in Niedersachsen (46), Christiane Luxem, Wirtschaftsstaatssekretärin in Rheinland-Pfalz (55), Thorsten Glauber, Umweltminister in Bayern (56), Alexander Jordan, CDU-MdB (45).

Sonntag: Sonja Lemke, Linken-MdB (35), Verena Schäffer, Familienministerin in NRW (40), Bettina Jarasch, Grünen-Fraktionsvorsitzende im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus (58).

FÜR SIE IN BERLIN UNTERWEGS

🗞️ Can you put a price on a grandkid?

20 November 2026 | Daily newsletter

͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌ ͏ ‌

Good morning,

I have more than one bone to pick with our ancestors about how their decisions from hundreds of years ago still affect us today, plus the overconfidence to think I'd win an argument with them about it. I still wouldn't want to face someone from centuries in the future and answer for what we did to the planet. In this week's long read, we do some uncomfortable math: what is their future worth to us today, and are we willing to pay for it?

Toyah Höher

Editor

Carbon pricing

How much are our great-great-great-great-grandkids worth?

Right now, the market decides.

〉 Read article 〉 Hide again

Tamara Kaňuchová, Belle de Jong

The year is 3026. One of your descendants, roughly 30 generations down the line, is heading to work. Maybe they live in a solarpunk paradise of green rooftops and take a fully electric bus. Or maybe they wake up in a sealed habitat and check the day's toxicity rating before strapping on an oxygen mask for the short walk to the underground commute, where they're safe from wildfire smoke and unpredictable storms raging above.

You’ll never meet them, and after so many generations, they likely won’t even carry your DNA. But they will have inherited something from you: up to 40% of the carbon dioxide emitted today will still be in the atmosphere when they’re born.

That carbon will shape the world they live in. So how do we account for the damage it will do to them? One way is to make emitting carbon cost money, which discourages pollution and raises funds for cleaner alternatives.

It’s the idea behind a familiar climate slogan: “Make polluters pay.” And the bill for not cutting emissions is already here: the floods that hit the Iberian Peninsula at the beginning of the year, for example, cost €7 billion in relief payments alone.

Those are bills we can already count. The harder part is the damage that hasn’t happened yet – which is still most of it – in a future we cannot exactly predict.

So how do we decide what a tonne of CO₂ should cost?

The answer involves economics, philosophy, politics, and a fair bit of guesswork.

Interest in reverse

Let’s start with economics: prices are determined by supply and demand. On the EU’s carbon market (the Emissions Trading System, or ETS), the EU controls supply: Brussels caps the number of carbon permits and lowers that cap every year.

The cap means companies have to compete for permits, pushing the price up. As the number shrinks each year, permits get scarcer and polluting gets more expensive.

On the demand side, a permit's price moves with the economy and energy prices. At the time of writing, a permit to emit one tonne of CO₂ costs around €85.

But those €85 aren't designed to make polluters pay for the harm they cause future generations. The price reflects what a permit is worth on the market, not the damage each tonne of CO₂ does.

That damage is called the social cost of carbon: the estimated harm of one extra tonne of CO₂ over its long lifetime of up to tens of thousands of years – from eroding ecosystems and melting ice sheets to climate disasters, failed harvests, and heat deaths.

Most of that harm, and the worst of it, will hit people who aren’t even born yet. So to factor it into a carbon price, we need to weigh damage decades or centuries away against the price we pay today.

Dominic Roser, a political philosopher and economist at the University of Fribourg, describes the dilemma like so: “Let’s say I know that climate change will destroy the window in my grandson’s house in 100 years, and the window will cost €100. Should I use €100 to buy an electric car instead of a fossil fuel car, or should I put €100 in the bank for it to grow, so my grandson will have much more money to buy a replacement window?”

The answer depends on how much that future €100 is worth to us today, and we tend to be impatient. Think of a mortgage: we prefer paying the bank interest to get a house now, rather than saving up for years. “People are psychologically hardwired to care less about the future than the present,” Roser said.

To calculate the social cost of carbon, economists capture this impatience in the so-called discount rate. It works like interest in reverse: the further away in the future a cost is, the less it counts today.

If you put €100 in the bank today at 1% interest, it'll be €101 next year. Discounting works the other way around: €100 next year is worth about €99 today. Because the discount compounds year after year, €100 a century from now is worth only about €37 today. So preventing a flood that will cause €100 of damage in 2126 is worth spending €37 on today. At a discount rate of 3%, the same flood is worth just €5 today.

Why the future gets a discount

So how do we determine the discount rate? Ottmar Edenhofer, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, breaks it down into three ingredients.

The first is the impatience we described. Economists call this the pure time preference rate: how much less we value something just because it comes later. At 0%, a person born in 2126 counts exactly as much as you do. Above that, they count for less, and the further into the future they're born, the less they count.

This is where philosophy comes in, and it's the most controversial ingredient: applied to climate, “it expresses a normative judgement about how you value future generations,” Edenhofer explained.

The second ingredient is economic growth. If our descendants are much wealthier than we are, as each generation has been for the past two centuries, they will be better able to bear the cost of climate damage. Asking today’s generation to pay the full cost of future damage would then be unfair, the argument goes. “It is not ethically okay to sacrifice the fate of the current generation on the altar of future generations,” said Edenhofer.

The third ingredient follows from the second: how much money is actually worth to people. The richer you are, the less an extra euro means to you. For a student, €100 is a lot, but for a millionaire, it's nothing. So if our descendants are wealthier, the same flood damage will cost them less than it would cost us.

Market versus morals

For two decades, the question of how much the future is worth has been debated by economists.

William Nordhaus, a Yale professor who shared the Nobel Prize in economics for his work on climate change, based his discount rate on the market: money in a savings account earns interest because people want a reward for waiting, so future damage should shrink at the same rate as savings grow.

He set the rate at which we value something less over time (the pure time preference rate) at 1.5%. That may sound small, but it means your descendant born a century from now counts for less than a quarter of you. His model also left out disasters and tipping points, so his carbon price came out low at USD 15 per tonne of CO₂.

Nicholas Stern, a former World Bank chief economist who advised the British government on climate change, rejected that approach on ethical grounds: being born later, he argued, is no reason for your wellbeing to count less. He set the pure time preference rate at just 0.1%, reflecting only the small chance that humanity will no longer exist – like if a meteorite struck the Earth. At that rate, your descendant in 100 years still counts for about 90% of you, and his carbon price came out at around USD 85 per tonne in 2006.

Edenhofer also questions Nordhaus’ reliance on the market to decide how much the future is worth. It'd only be justified “if we could assume that the current capital market takes into account all the future climate risks,” he said, “and this is not the case.”

Markets ignore so-called fat tail events: rare but extreme disasters far outside historical patterns, like the 2008 financial crisis. In a warming world, “it could be a dramatic heat wave, it could be a drought, it could be a flood,” Edenhofer said. “I doubt that the capital market is an institution which allows us to take into account the future risk.”

What a tonne really costs

Today's markets, in other words, are a poor guide to what the future is worth. What a tonne of CO₂ should cost depends on the damage it does to society, Rick van der Ploeg, an economist at the University of Oxford, explained.

For that, he said, the key concept is the social cost of carbon, which includes slowly falling productivity, a higher chance of disasters, and a growing risk of reaching irreversible tipping points. When factoring in the “strong interaction between the biosphere, climate, and land”, the social cost of carbon rises dramatically, Edenhofer said.

Even a conservative estimate puts it far above today’s €85. For a tonne emitted in 2026, the German Environment Agency (UBA) puts the social cost at €1,000 if all generations count equally (a 0% pure time preference rate), or €350 if today’s generation is weighted slightly more (a 1% pure time preference rate).

UBA’s model doesn’t count tipping points, extreme weather, lost productivity, migration, conflict, or the loss of biodiversity. Including them, the agency writes, would likely raise its estimates at least tenfold.

So why doesn’t the EU simply charge polluters €350 or €1,000 a tonne, and make them pay for the full damage they cause, now and in the future?

The economists at the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change concluded that the social cost of carbon was too uncertain to set a price on, said Edenhofer. So policymakers set a limit on global warming instead – 1.5°C, or 2°C at most – which translates into a budget of how much CO₂ we can still emit.

The EU takes the same approach: it sets a cap on emissions based on its climate targets, and the market finds the price within it. That has one big advantage, Roser said: it doesn’t require anyone to decide whether future generations count equally.

Does it work?

On its own terms, yes. The cap guarantees that emissions fall, whatever the price. Emissions from the sectors covered by the ETS have halved since 2005, while the EU economy has grown overall. “The EU is the first economic region which has shown that economic growth can be decoupled from emissions growth,” said Edenhofer, calling the ETS “a huge success story”.

Quickly, though, the moral question comes back, and politics sneaks in again. Where should we set the cap? Most policymakers, Roser said, would rather think: “As long as we leave [future generations] a decent and habitable planet, it’s okay if we look after ourselves.”

What counts as “decent and habitable” is up for negotiation – and globally, current policies are heading for around 2.8°C of warming. “This is a value judgement, but if you want to avoid future catastrophes with a very high likelihood, it is not good enough,” said Edenhofer.

Caps can also be loosened. A rising carbon price is the system doing its job, but industry worries about competitiveness and consumers feel it in their bills. “Either you want to achieve the cap, then you have to accept the price, or you cannot accept the price,” said Edenhofer.

Some governments already can’t. In June, EU countries and the European Parliament agreed that starting in 2028, the number of extra permits released into the new carbon market for transport and heating (ETS2) whenever the price exceeds €45 a tonne will be doubled, after France and Czechia warned about rising fuel bills. Moves like these make carbon cheaper, and indirectly answer how much the future is worth to us.

So what is the future worth?

Edenhofer compared the question to walking along a cliff: “You want to understand how far away you want to be from the cliff to have a safe walk.” The closer we get to the edge, the cheaper our path, but the bigger the risk of a fall we can’t undo.

On the other side of the path lies a second danger: climate policy so costly that it causes social unrest. The challenge, Edenhofer said, is to steer clear of both. Whether your descendant in 3026 lives in a solarpunk paradise or underground depends on how much distance from the edge we’re willing to pay for today.

Life's cheaper in the east

A few weeks ago, I had a train to catch from an Ostbahnhof – the East Station – of a large German city. The area around it felt rougher than the neighbourhoods next to it: a few loveless shopfronts, run-down streets.

It wasn’t the first time I’d noticed this at an Ostbahnhof, and it left me wondering. Are the eastern sides of cities generally worse off?

There may be something to it. Some cities such as London and Paris have known east-west divides, and researchers studying English cities have found that some of these divides are, in part, a legacy of industrial air pollution. In the late 19th century, the prevailing winds carried factory smoke eastwards. Those who could afford it settled in the cleaner west, and the east stayed poorer. Long after the factories closed, rents there are still cheaper.

But the pattern doesn’t hold everywhere. In Brussels, the east is the wealthier side. And in Berlin, the poorer east probably owes more to a different historical divide, the city’s split during the Cold War.

Sebastian Gräff

Last but not least

If you haven't had enough of all the numbers, I invite you to dive deeper into the subject with this book, which focuses on so-called “fat-tailed” events, or black swans, as author Nassim Nicholas Taleb describes them in The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable.

The name comes from the old European assumption that all swans were white, which people believed until sailors working for the Dutch East India Company came across black swans in Australia in 1697.

I find Taleb's idea that we tend to act as though we've always “seen it coming” only after major crises occur (think market crashes or even terrorist attacks) quite fascinating. It might change the way you think about the world.

Tamara Kaňuchová

NEWSLETTER · 20 Nov 2026, 00:10

What Is This, Y2K?

Why everything keeps breaking, plus: the Global Briefing news quiz, the dangers of investigating, leaderless Iran?, and ‘Mississippi miracle’ …

ADVERTISEMENT

Thursday, November 19, 2026 View in browser

Insights, analysis and must reads from CNN’s Fareed Zakaria and the Global Public Square team, compiled by Global Briefing editor Chris Good

Seeing this newsletter as a forward? Sign up here.

What Is This, Y2K?

Amid a series of high-profile service outages, “Americans have begun to wonder if their country is actually breaking,” The New York Times’ Sabrina Tavernise, Georgia Gee and Madaleine Rubin write. The comparison to Y2K is tempting, but the biggest underlying problem today is different and potentially more persistent.

Last Thursday, a massive Microsoft outage disrupted office work. A day later, the FAA grounded all domestic flights. Outages at Apple and major US banks followed, producing a sense that America’s software is suddenly AWOL. “The cascading series of tech failures left Americans stranded in airports, refreshing their work computers, and generally scratching their heads over what was actually happening,” as the Times reporters put it.

Several observers, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, have likened this moment to the Y2K bug, which was supposed to threaten all manner of critical systems when the calendar flipped to year 2000. Computer code had expressed years in only two digits, and software systems could think it was 1900. In the end, nothing came of it. Y2K was “one bug and one day … to get through it,” Nadella said Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported. Today, AI is making things more complicated in an entirely new way.

Both hackers and defenders are using AI tools to find vulnerabilities, The Wall Street Journal’s Robert McMillan writes. An outage doesn’t have to be the result of an attack; it can be the result of a messy patch, intended to fix software before hackers find a vulnerability and exploit it. “Behind the scenes,” McMillan writes, “there have been relentless AI-driven cyberattacks, an avalanche of software patches amid Bugmageddon”—a tidal wave of software bugs revealed by AI models searching for them—“sleepless nights for IT staffers and so much cybersecurity work that incident responders are turning away business. While outages are nothing new, AI has created a pressure cooker that makes it difficult to discern cybersecurity threats from the ceaseless updates that amount to their remedy.” Tim Starks writes for CyberScoop: “there’s a growing sense that patching fueled by a race to close vulnerabilities uncovered by artificial intelligence was a contributing factor.”

Broadly, cybersecurity involves a race between hackers and defenders (or “white hats”), who hunt for vulnerabilities for opposite purposes. Historically, software companies have offered “bug bounties” to anyone who can find and report vulnerabilities, so they can be patched before hackers unearth them. AI appears to have sped up this constant competition.

The cause of the recent outages is probably “a combination of a few things, all happening at once,” cybersecurity researcher Daniel Miessler posted to X. AI tools have allowed new hackers to emerge, and existing hackers are now able to attempt attacks at a larger scale, which is “forcing massive (and dangerous) patching.” To an extent, it’s a story about AI making work easier: “What a lot of people don’t understand about ‘hacking’ is that it’s largely a whole lot of overhead,” Miessler writes. “Doing extensive research. Launching scans. Finding relationships between entities. … [I]t’s hard and tedious and time-consuming to do that well. So there were very few attackers doing it.” AI has made all of that “5-100X” easier, Miessler writes.

At the same time, Chris Stokel-Walker writes for Scientific American, our software systems have gotten more complex over the years. That means a patch in one area is more likely to affect another area unpredictably. Cybersecurity practitioner Wickey Wang writes for her Chasing Polaris newsletter that the FAA and Microsoft outages “illustrate how infrastructure changes and complex system dependencies can disrupt critical services,” even when no cyberattack is involved. “For companies, the lesson is that preventing attacks is only part of the job. Keeping the business running when something goes wrong matters just as much.”

ADVERTISEMENT

Missile Money

Throughout the wars in Ukraine and Iran, military analysts have noted a disadvantageous arbitrage. Russia and Iran can attack with relatively cheap drones, but Western aerial defenses are expensive. In defending themselves, Ukraine and Gulf Arab countries have expended pricey missiles fending off cheap drones—a financial loss every time.

About how much does one Patriot interceptor missile cost?

a) $800,000

b) $4 million

c) $6 million

d) $8 million

To see the answer, read to the end of this newsletter.

The Limits of ‘Accountability’

Congressional investigations might carry risks

Could pursuing a slew of investigations into the Trump administration backfire on Democrats? “They need to tell a coherent story … without turning President Trump into a martyr,” Emily Bazelon of The New York Times Magazine and Yale Law School told Fareed on Sunday’s GPS.

Leaderless Iran?

The Iranian public has not seen or heard Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei since he was elevated to that role in March. In April, Reuters reported (citing unnamed sources) that the Iranian leader had disfiguring wounds to his face and leg, suffered in the airstrike that killed his father at the war’s outset.

Iranians “are discovering life without” a cleric political figure dominating their country, The Economist writes. “The most important shift is in the way the regime wields power. ‘What’s principally changed is that there’s no clear, final arbiter,’ says Sanam Vakil of Chatham House, a London-based think-tank. … Instead, six men, all from the ranks of the Supreme National Security Council, a 13-man body of generals and bureaucrats, dominate decision-making. … The biggest decisions require the collective’s consent. These include matters such as negotiations about ending or restarting the war with America, nuclear policy, or the appointment of a non-cleric as intelligence minister for the first time in decades. But each individual also has a degree of autonomy.” President Masoud Pezeshkian, for instance, “has largely been left to manage a war-induced depression and a currency in near freefall.”

In its speculative, 2027 look-ahead issue, The Economist writes that Iran’s military leaders, particularly in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), are poised to grow more powerful. The ongoing war will “hasten the IRGC generals’ ascent to power,” the magazine predicts. “No one will be quite sure when the theocracy has passed. State television will continue its standard diet of Koranic recitations. But the clerics who have led the Islamic Republic since its inception in 1979 will recede further from view.”

‘Mississippi Miracle’

Now that Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, commentators continue to marvel at the result in a deep-red state that had not sent a Black senator to Washington since Reconstruction. In The New Yorker, Mississippian Paige Williams writes that some Mississippi Democrats have hoped the drawn-out, down-to-the-wire vote-counting would call attention to Mississippi voting procedures, as the integration of Experian data required some voters to cast “affidavit” ballots when their data didn’t match.

Williams also notes the long, intertwined, violent history of voting and race in Mississippi, listing some of the 20th century civil-rights activists who were murdered by racist vigilantes for encouraging or attempting to register Black people to vote. The viciousness of that history makes Colom’s victory all the more notable. “Forrest County, in southern Mississippi, is named for Nathan Bedford Forrest, the Klan’s grand wizard,” Williams writes. “Colom flipped it.”

News Quiz: The Answer Is …

Question: About how much does one Patriot interceptor missile cost? Answer: $4 million

Four-million-dollar Patriot missiles aren’t the only way to shoot down an incoming Russian or Iranian drone. Helicopters and planes can loiter or launch, downing drones with air-to-air missiles.

More promisingly, Ukraine has developed interceptor drones—and in April made a deal to export them to Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar. Trading drone for drone is a much better cost equation, and it seems to be where things are headed in the world of weaponry.

Profiling interceptor-drone startups in Europe, James Paton writes for The New York Times that “governments are calling on” such companies “to help plug gaps in the region’s air defenses. The [defense] industry is under pressure to increase production, lower costs and keep pace with threats that continue to evolve. Many companies are forging partnerships in Ukraine to capitalize on the country’s military technology expertise and gain crucial insights from the front line.” Larger incumbents are working on the technology, too. “A proposed Europe-Ukraine air defense system, called Freyja, is one part of [Europe’s developing drone-defense] strategy,” Paton writes. “The project could help reduce the region’s dependence on the United States and provide a lower-cost alternative to American Patriot interceptors.”

Lasers also seem promising. Russia is now using jet-powered attack drones, and speed is one of the engineering challenges faced by interceptor designers.

“In the first 100 hours after Operation Epic Fury began against Iran on February 28th 2026, America fired interceptors worth an estimated $1.7bn,” The Economist points out. The outlook is expected to improve. Drone startups and lasers aside, Lockheed is also working to make a Patriot interceptor missile that’s 90% as effective for half the cost, The Economist writes. “[I]n 2027 the economics of air defence will become less grievous. Cheaper systems will enter production or service. Others will be made in greater numbers, bringing down costs.”

What A Day: DOGE Bites Man

Bad mistakes, Elon Musk has made a few.

Matt Berg

Nov 19

READ IN APP

THIS MUSK BE THE PLACE

Elon Musk now insists that he’s not MAGA. Donald Trump isn’t thrilled.

What will become of MAGA on the day after President Donald Trump slinks from the Oval Office for the final time? We may have just gotten a hint: Some who leapt proudly onto the MAGA bandwagon will insist that, actually, they were never really all that into it.

So it goes for the guy who once styled himself as Trump’s “First Buddy.” Americans woke up to Broligarch Elon Musk gaslighting the world, insisting that he’s not a big fan of the MAGA movement at all — despite all the public evidence to the contrary and hundreds of millions of dollars spent on failed pro-Trump candidates.

“I’m not MAGA. Well, at least I’m not, like, I’m not sure what MAGA means,” Musk sputtered during an interview at the New York Times DealBook Summit. “I think there are positives and negatives in both parties.”

I don’t know who Musk thinks he’s fooling. This is the same guy who exclaimed two years ago: “I am not just MAGA. I’m dark, gothic MAGA.” The dude who spent almost half a billion dollars backing Republicans in the midterms? (A “pretty foolish” move, he now admits.) Musk used to wander the White House and participate in meetings while wearing a hat that read: “Trump was right about everything.” And who can forget when Musk jumped awkwardly on stage, because he was so hyped during Trump’s campaign?

All that goes down the memory hole, now that the Democrats are empowered in Washington D.C. and in Texas, where much of Musk’s business empire lives.

Federal employees affected by Musk’s chaotic DOGE initiative, which tanked morale in the federal government and didn’t save nearly as much money as he estimated, aren’t amused by the broligarch’s switchup.

“What a sad, pathetic man,” Tyler Creighton, a member of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau union, told What A Day. Musk’s team tried to “delete” the financial watchdog — and failed.

Trump called Musk a “friend” today, but also gave him a warning.

Unlike Musk, Trump said the meaning of MAGA is no mystery. “MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well,” Trump told NBC News. (I can picture fictional mob boss Tony Soprano, puffing a cigar, warning his buddies that people who turn on him “don’t do well.”)

Everyone knows what “MAGA” really means to Donald Trump. It means: Donald Trump.

Trump’s thinly veiled threat comes as tech bros reconsider their allegiances after Democrats swept the midterms. Top Dems in the House and Senate are gearing up to investigate Trump’s allies and their enablers — which will likely include tech companies that assisted with his aggressive deportation agenda and donated millions to his vanity projects.

Musk isn’t the first to signal a break with MAGA. Palantir CEO Alex Karp drew attention earlier this month when he described himself as a “progressive” who has “been a Democrat my whole life.” In reality, Karp donated $1 million to a super PAC supporting Trump, and his company has been a key partner for ICE in targeting immigrants.

Hilariously, Musk’s SpaceX now seems to have stopped using the MAGA term “Gulf of America” in its press releases. The company briefly posted the traditional “Gulf of Mexico,” then reverted to just “the Gulf.” You’ll have to try harder than that, Elon!

WHAT ELSE? 👀

Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the nation’s top cybersecurity agency wouldn’t say whether the Capitol insurrection occurred, and insisted that whatever happened wasn’t an “attack” of any kind. “Was there an attack on the Capitol on January 6?” Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) asked Michael LoSapio, a Palantir executive tapped to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, during his confirmation hearing today. “I don’t know,” he responded. “No, I don’t believe it was an attack. No.” Blumenthal was dumbfounded: “Were you alive on the planet?”

Trump’s meeting today with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian dictator Vladimir Putin yielded no major breakthroughs — but the hangout seems to have brought Trump even closer to his favorite authoritarian pal. “Who is he?” Trump chuckled, pointing to Putin. He walked over to Putin and shook his hand: “It’s my friend.”

Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in 2017, the U.N.’s International Court of Justice ruled today. The landmark judgement could shape how the court handles such cases moving forward, including South Africa’s accusation that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Kirkland & Ellis, the largest law firm in the country, conducted about 6,491 hours of free work for the Trump administration — valued at $11.8 million, according to documents provided to Congress. Trump “successfully reshaped the firm into a tool of the state,” the New York Times writes.

Jared Kushner’s private equity firm, Affinity, owns a $32 million stake in a U.S. defense contractor that has benefited immensely from the Russia-Ukraine war and conflicts in the Middle East since Trump took office, The Atlantic reports, citing recent public filings. “One of the questions he’s faced is why nearly all of the money that Affinity has raised comes from Gulf royals with an existential stake in the results of his diplomacy,” the outlet writes. “He now faces a new question: Why would a man working for peace be seeking to profit from war?”

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin had been doing such a bad job at explaining the recent tech outages that White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller sidelined him from making more TV appearances, Politico reports. Maybe Mullin can focus on solving the bed bug crisis at FEMA instead?

What should the newly-minted millionaires and billionaires do with their wealth following Anthropic’s record-breaking public offering? Curbed put together a list of 34 ways rich people could help New York City, from funding a music teacher and full band in every middle school, to building a floating pool in the East River. I enjoyed reading this, even if I have little faith that these people will do much good with their cash.

LIGHT AT THE END… ☀️

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA) rejected Trump’s nominee to lead the National Science Foundation, saying that the candidate “did not do enough to stand up for science and against irresponsible decisions and statements.” Is Cassidy finally standing up to Trump? Better late than never, I guess.

A new project led by a Sweden-based institute is collecting Greenland residents’ personal stories about their childhoods and homes, as climate change reshapes the country. An exhibit linked to the project called Ilulissat’s Icefjord Center, opened in September.

Pope Leo picked up a baby dressed like him during a popemobile ride through St. Peter’s Square in Vatican City. Very adorable content here.

A woman from New York ran the World Marathon Majors this year — seven marathons around the world — while pregnant. That wasn’t her plan, but when she learned about the baby, she didn’t want to change her goal of completing all the races in 12 months. “I want to teach my son resilience and that he can do hard things,” she told the Associated Press.

A 90-year-old Texas woman teaches one-hour fitness classes six days a week, which have become so popular that the community center had to limit the classes to 80 people. Another amazing fact: She became a fitness instructor at 75 years old. “I wish I could reach more people,” she told the Washington Post. “Everyone should get up and exercise.”

Parents are losing their minds over a phenomenon sweeping the nation: Kids’ school photos often look more like mug shots. “We’re in the midst of a no-smile epidemic,” the Wall Street Journal reports. One 11-year-old girl explained what’s going on: “A big smile just looks cringe now,” she said. “It looks like you’re trying too hard. A straight face or a tiny smile looks more chill.”

John Fetterman’s Days Seem Numbered—and He Knows It

The cantankerous Democrat is now irrelevant. His colleagues think that’s all the more reason to kick him out.

Joe Perticone • FREE PREVIEW

READ TO ME

Today’s edition is about John Fetterman, the Pennsylvania senator whose Democratic colleagues would like to see him leave Congress and not come back. Several House Democrats are mulling giving him a primary challenge in 2028, with some already making secret moves to better position themselves. I spoke about the situation with Fetterman himself, and he appeared to get quite upset.

In addition, organizations looking to take advantage of your enthusiasm for various 2028 presidential candidates are already building out their faux political action committees. I’ll teach you how to tell a real PAC from a fake one to help you stay clear of an avalanche of unnecessary emails and text messages over the next two years. Lastly, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI has brought out some vintage conservative feelings on Capitol Hill. All that and more, below.

(Photo illustration by Sarah Rogers/The Bulwark | Photos: Getty, Shutterstock)

Call of duty: Pennsylvania

If you squint—or, really, just look straight at it—the behavior of Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) over the past few years seems like a long, needlessly complex process of baiting a primary challenge in 2028. If that was his plan, it seems to be working out quite well.

Earlier this fall, Fetterman addressed the Republican midterm convention in Dallas via a recorded video, which angered his Democratic colleagues. Later, he began sending fundraising appeals using Republican email lists. At the Texas Tribune festival in September, Fetterman mistakenly referred to himself as a “lifelong Republican.” He appears regularly on Fox News either to trash his colleagues or to threaten to leave the Democratic party.

Fetterman wouldn’t have to quit anything if he got the boot first, and several House Democrats are considering a 2028 primary challenge to help make that happen. There are also Democrats back in Pennsylvania who are eager to compete for his seat. A House Democrat told me ...

The Adversarial: Handshakes Without Headway

An update on the world's greatest security threats ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌

Image: President of Russia via Wikimedia Commons

Welcome to The Adversarial. Every other week, we'll provide you with expert analysis on America's greatest challengers: China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and jihadists. Read more below.

> Iran

Washington and Tehran are stuck in a loop, with no indication that they are engaged in talks — although Iran has continued meeting with mediators. Following a G7 meeting, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the U.S. economic pressure campaign — including sanctions, an ongoing naval blockade, and newer efforts to block Iran from transporting weapons and sanctioned items by land — is “working so well that the president really doesn’t have any need to conduct major combat operations.”

However, Rubio refused to provide any sort of timeline, which highlights a fundamental problem for Washington: no clear objective. Does Washington hope that economic and fiscal pressure will eventually lead to some amorphous type of uprising that overthrows the regime? Or does the Trump administration plan to economically squeeze Iran until it agrees to U.S. demands regarding its nuclear program and other issues? It is unclear how any of this would happen, given Tehran’s proven ability to withstand major pressure and unwillingness to make major concessions.

Iran still has options and is unlikely to accept indefinite pressure. It could use the time that Washington might allow for economic pressure to take effect to rebuild its missile and drone arsenals and even try to reconstitute its nuclear program. Or Tehran could escalate attacks in the region, increase cyber attacks, and engage in more “gray zone” tactics in Europe and North America to break out of Washington’s stranglehold on its economy. Any of these actions could lead the United States to resume major military strikes. Each side sees any concession as an indication of weakness and therefore is likely to respond to pressure from the other with hardened resolve.

Furthermore, it’s not entirely clear that the administration has chosen a patient approach of economic pressure. Reporting suggests that U.S. President Donald Trump is still considering a new wave of hostilities. In the meantime, the United States struck Qeshm Island on Tuesday, and tit-for-tat strikes between the two countries have continued in the region. The situation remains fragile.

Secretary Marco Rubio speaks with U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband during the G7 family photo with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha in Paris, France, Nov. 10, 2026. Image: U.S. Department of State via Wikimedia Commons

> China

General Secretary Xi Jinping scored some major image points this week, hosting a summit with Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, who were both in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Multiple photos showed Xi standing between Trump and Putin, serving Beijing’s interest in showing itself as an equal power. However, the summit appears to have achieved little of substance.

The scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang continues to fester as the other most important topic in U.S.-Chinese relations this week. Despite controversy surrounding whether Alice Huang was a spy for China, the indisputable fact is that billions of dollars in Nvidia chips under U.S. export control measures have been leaked to China. The case will set off a chain reaction, further tightening China’s access to advanced U.S. semiconductor chips. It also revealed the hard truth that — regardless of the billions of dollars the Chinese state has invested in its domestic chip industry — China continues to rely on advanced American chips for the development of its high-tech sectors, including AI.

The U.S. midterm elections brought a “blue wave” that shook the Republican Party’s grip on the legislative branch. In early 2027, the new Congress will start pushing back against Trump’s accommodation-oriented China policy. The Huang case has already set off several revelations about the internal splits within the Trump administration on tech-control policies toward China. These rifts are bound to expand, deepen, and drive China policy in a different direction.

The “NVIDIA NV40” graphics processor, March 17, 2018. Image: Martijn Boer via Wikimedia Commons

> Russia

If negotiations never end, did they ever really start? The U.S.-led Russo-Ukrainian peace negotiations experienced another flurry of activity last week. But while the U.S. side, led by Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, insists that it is making progress, the sense in Ukraine and Europe is that meaningful talks with Russia never really began. Europeans see little evidence that Russia is serious about negotiations and instead see Moscow using the meetings to try to turn the United States against Ukraine and Europe. In this vein, Russia pushed to expand the talks to address the existing “European security architecture” and called for NATO to roll back its expansion to pre-1997 boundaries. In response, European leaders insisted that they have a seat at the table, given that all this very much involves them.

The problem is that Europe has not fully integrated its foreign policy, leaving it with a hybrid arrangement that keeps everyone who is not inside the Brussels bubble terribly confused. Further complicating the picture, rather than one European “seat at the table,” Europe suggested seven seats, with representatives from five countries plus the European Commission and the European Council all now representing Europe.

What makes Europe’s diplomatic mess problematic is that Europe’s involvement is crucial for any peace talks to have real impact. This is because Europe — not the United States — is now Ukraine’s primary financial and military backer. Ukraine’s most recent successful strike on the Kerch Bridge was partly facilitated by Dutch defense technology that had been fused into Ukraine’s deep-strike missile program. The European Union and its member states are allocating more than $50 billion per year and keeping Ukraine’s economy and military afloat. Europe is no longer an ancillary player in this war and will have to be central to any real peace negotiations. For now, those serious negotiations appear a long way off.

European Council Meeting Room, Dec. 16, 2017. Image: EU2017EE Estonian Presidency via Wikimedia Commons

> North Korea

Trump’s November trip to China intensified speculation of another meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Trump has repeatedly declared his interest in resuming dialogue, even suggesting that Washington had been in contact with Pyongyang and that Kim wanted to re-engage. However, behind the scenes, there are indications that there has been no significant U.S. contact with North Korea since the last bilateral meeting in 2019. North Korea emphasized that it expects U.S. concessions prior to any meeting, including abandoning Washington’s denuclearization policy and reducing Washington’s “hostile policy,” which encompasses a lengthy list of North Korean security and economic demands. Unsurprisingly, Trump did meet with Kim this week.

Pyongyang is in a far stronger strategic position than during Trump’s previous meetings with Kim, negating its need for diplomatic, security, or economic benefits from Washington. The regime is receiving massive economic benefits from Russia, enjoying enhanced trade with China, and undertaking lucrative cybercrimes.

Kim may calculate that the devastating midterm election results will entice Trump toward grandiose foreign policy endeavors to burnish his legacy and thus be more malleable to North Korean demands. But Pyongyang would question Trump’s ability to implement any promises in the face of a more resistant Congress under Democratic control. Short of a significant U.S. initiative, Pyongyang will continue to wait while augmenting its nuclear, missile, and conventional weapon arsenals.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un tours the Nampo Shipyard, Nov. 2, 2026. Image: KCNA

> Jihadists

Epidemics and terrorist groups both feed off instability. Today in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), an Islamic State affiliate is accelerating the second-largest Ebola outbreak in history, and the disease in turn reinforces the instability that fuels extremism and violence. The Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) — also known as the Islamic State Central Africa Province — pledged allegiance to the Islamic State in 2019 and has become one of the deadliest nonstate actors in the world. The ADF and other armed groups in the region have a history of kidnapping health workers and attacking health facilities, which has complicated efforts to move assistance into the region of eastern DRC where the ADF and Ebola are particularly active. For example, from Nov. 5 to 6, ADF militants attacked the village of Cantine-Aloya, where dozens of Ebola patients were receiving treatment. The attack forced residents — including Ebola patients — to flee. The ADF’s actions are helping to spread Ebola while undermining efforts to contain the outbreak.

More than 100 other armed groups operate in the DRC, as well as Ugandan and Congolese forces, but the relatively small ADF punches above its weight in inflicting terror on the local population and is notable for its connection to the global jihadist movement. While the group previously benefitted from Islamic State financing, it no longer relies on the global group, instead funding itself through gold trafficking and other activities. This self-reliance decreases the effectiveness of sanctions, leaving outside actors with few effective tools to counter the ADF.

Workers unload medical supplies from a cargo plane at Beni airport in North Kivu, Aug. 5, 2018. Image: MONUSCO via Wikimedia Commons

The Ground Beneath the Cloud: Dispersion and Dependency in the Digital Age

The Ground Beneath the Cloud: Dispersion and Dependency in the Digital Age. Commercial cloud architecture has made digital infrastructure more resilient to localized disruption. Geographic dispersion, workload migration, and failover have allowed providers to preserve access in instances of degradation or even destruction. Yet, underpinning this resiliency are interlocking dependencies on access to energy, supply chains, and governing bodies that extend well beyond the data centers hosting the commercial cloud. The United States is building digital capacity — data centers and the underlying systems supporting them — faster than the governance frameworks needed to orchestrate the public agencies, private operators, and the physical infrastructure on which that capacity depends. Grand Theft Life

Plus, your next iPhone is getting a glow-up.

November 19, 2026View Online | Sign Up | Shop

Presented By

Make scents of this. What does a newborn baby smell like? According to an AI trained by professional sniffers (yes, that’s a job that exists), it’s apparently…a plate of Barilla spaghetti. And that’s not even the strangest part of this gloriously weird story from MIT Technology Review—in a lab near Newark Liberty International Airport, about 30 human sniffers are “slowly working their way through every odor on Earth” to train what one AI startup calls the first foundation model for smell. One outside expert warns the AI could still miss some context though: For example, Camembert cheese and used diapers share a molecule. Let’s not mix those up.

We review two of the new Kindles.

Could AI’s official church be…a Buddhist monastery?

What Elon Musk thinks about his $500 million US midterms bet.

—Lindsey Choo, Whizy Kim, and Saira Mueller

Breaking

Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq today with a higher-than-expected share price, making it the biggest IPO on record. And not just that: Its shares shot up by more than 30% at one point (they’re up by about 18% as of publication), sending its value to around $2 trillion and placing it within the largest 10 companies by market value. While it could come back down, it’s an early sign of how much enthusiasm there is for AI—and for Claude specifically.

The Download

How a $1 billion video game simulates real life

Rockstar Games

TL;DR: This isn’t your grandma’s Grand Theft Auto game (but, ironically, it might be the one she’s most interested in). The latest installment in the series, which came out today, appears to be a life simulator that pushes the limits of how obsessively detailed a virtual world can be. And it involves plenty of sharp satire on all the tech we use every day.

What happened: This is how big a moment Grand Theft Auto VI is: Already nearing an estimated $2 billion in revenue, the game (which retails for $79.99 for the standard edition) is now projected to earn more in its launch week than Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour did in 21 months. And while the series is famous as a virtual playground for stealing cars and committing other chaotic crimes, the newest entry is much more than that: It lets you live a whole other life doing chores, doomscrolling, and pursuing hobbies in its fictional version of Florida.

Here’s a taste of all the law-abiding activities in the game:

Doing home renovation, from fixing the leaky roof to painting your bedroom wall.

Going bird-watching (there are 62 different avian species to log).

If you’d rather not touch grass, you can scroll social media on your extremely detailed in-game smartphone (called an iFruit, naturally).

Oh, and you can go Jet Skiing with a dog—who, by the way, is driving the thing (which might admittedly be less law-abiding).

Uncanny valley: Every GTA game is a biting satire of society, and in 2026, that means a world littered with knockoffs of all the tech we use. Aside from the aforementioned iFruit phone, GTA VI’s version of Amazon is called Sahara; instead of Uber, there’s a rideshare app called RydeMe, and an app called BuckMe works like your mobile banking app (with Zelle). There’s even an AI-powered car scanner that flags which vehicles have GPS trackers and what their resale value would be.

How fake Florida got built: Cramming this much detail into one game is arguably a technological feat in itself. GTA VI reportedly cost more than $1 billion and took an army of nearly 5,000 people about a decade to make. Rockstar, the game’s developer, even set up a separate office just to create its roughly 30,000 unique NPCs—the non-playable characters who populate the background of the world. The game has over 600,000 animations for characters to act out, and the physics are so realistic that individual strands of hair react to movement. And, per Rockstar, no generative AI was used to create this level of fidelity.

Bottom line: Unfortunately, GTA VI is hard to play in its full glory right now. The PlayStation 5 Pro, the console that runs it best, is nearly impossible to find at retail price. But, given all the hype and its blockbuster sales, you’ll probably be hearing about it for a while, even if you never go for a drive yourself. —WK

Sponsored By Celigo

Oh look, another AI agent

Hey, pal. Refreshments are to your left. But before we do intros, here’s an important point courtesy of Celigo: Every new AI agent adds another way of reaching data, systems, and business processes. Without a common foundation underneath, AI can make an already fragmented enterprise less unified. Kinda awkward.

Celigo notes that production-ready AI needs three things: access to the systems it acts on, context that explains what the data means, and controls that define what it’s allowed to do. Without all three, it's another source of risk. Their POV: AI works best when your systems move as one.

And look, they’ve written a paper on this very subject.

Crafted for CIOs and AI leaders, the paper can show you why more autonomy isn’t better automation. Check out the foundation that can fix fragmentation for good.

Turning the page on my old Kindle

Disclosure: Companies may send us products to test, but they never pay for our opinions. Our recommendations are unbiased and unfiltered, and Tech Brew may earn a commission if you buy through our links.

I’m a certified e-reader loyalist: I want to carry a hefty fantasy novel without staring at my glowing phone, and I want it to fit in my tiny purse. I’ve hung on to my old Kindle Basic 2019 for years for the most boring reason possible—nothing is wrong with it.

I was skeptical that a new Kindle could improve my life, since my old one was doing the job just fine. But then I saw the lineup’s new colors and sleek redesign, and suddenly “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” sounded like something my husband made up.

How we tested them: Over a month, I read at least two full-length books each on the Kindle Colorsoft ($320) and Paperwhite ($250) Signature Editions, one with the Page-Turn Cover ($80) on and one without. I brought them with me everywhere—on the subway, to coffee shops, to the park, and to bed. I borrow most of my books from my local library through the Libby app, so I just sent them straight to my Kindle account, and they synced to every Kindle I own. The cover, which snaps on magnetically, has physical buttons I can press to turn pages. And to see what color actually adds, I flipped through a cookbook on the Colorsoft.

The Kindle Colorsoft with the page turn cover on is on the left. On the right is the Kindle Paperwhite. Lindsey Choo/Morning Brew Inc.

The Good: Both Kindles are very customizable—you can tweak the font, brightness, and warmth to your liking. They also respond much faster to the touch, and library books that used to take a few minutes to load on my old Kindle showed up almost immediately. The battery life was impressive: Each device still had more than half of its battery left after reading the two books, while my old Kindle tapped out every two books or so. The colors on the Colorsoft were slightly muted but plenty vivid for book covers and visual elements.

The Bad: At 7 inches, the new Kindles are a bit bigger than my old 6-inch one. That’s great for screen space, but as they’re made of aluminum, it also means they’re heavier: At 8.1 ounces, they weigh about 2 ounces more (roughly the weight of a tennis ball) than my old one, and are harder to hold with one hand. Having physical buttons with the cover is lovely, but the default button setup was so annoying (the top button turns forward, which forced me to reach my thumb up each time) that I had to dig into the settings to swap them. At $80, the cover felt more like a nice-to-have than a game changer (it’s also only compatible with the already pricier Signature Editions).

Verdict: ✅ Signal—for the Paperwhite (for everyday readers) and Colorsoft (for pretty gadget lovers). ❌ Noise—for the Page-Turn Cover, which didn’t earn its price tag. —LC

The Zeitbyte

These Buddhist monks want to become AI’s official church

Morning Brew Inc., Photo: Unsplash

If you had to guess which group wants to become the official church of AI, you’d probably picture a cadre of Bay Area engineers who’ve had one too many existential late-night convos with Claude. But the actual answer is a Buddhist monastery nestled deep in the woods of northern Vermont.

At first glance, life at the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth (MAPLE for short) is low-key and low-tech: Someone physically rings a loud bell to wake residents at 4am. Everyone chants and meditates for an hour each, and then a simple breakfast is served (boiled cabbage and beans, with vinegar being the only flavoring used).

But MAPLE’s mission is actually extremely 2026: stopping Silicon Valley from causing an AI apocalypse. The order’s founder believes that the tech bros are developing AI out of a “religious fervor” that worships data and numbers. One monastery visitor even dismisses Strava, the fitness tracking app, as a “cult.” As The New Yorker’s profile slowly reveals, though, MAPLE itself turns out to be a strange, secretive place where absolutely everything’s recorded or monitored—even the monks’ breathing, apparently. Strava, at least, lets you turn off the tracking. —WK

Snapshot of the day

November 19, 2026

Sidharth Bhatia, Kalrav Joshi, Anirudh S.K.

Celebrations erupted in Rohingya refugee camps across Bangladesh as the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during the military crackdown of 2017. In a historic verdict, the world’s highest court, for the first time, held a state responsible for genocide, with nine of its 15 judges finding that “the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya”. The military campaign forced more than 700,000 Rohingya Muslims to flee to Bangladesh amid reports of mass killings, gang rapes and the burning of villages. Crowds watching the verdict on outdoor screens broke into applause as the ruling was announced.

The verdict also puts New Delhi’s continued engagement with Myanmar’s military junta under an uncomfortable spotlight. India has maintained formal ties with the regime since the 2021 coup and backed its electoral exercise despite widespread questions over its legitimacy. The Modi government must now reckon with the implications of standing alongside a regime held responsible for genocide by the world’s highest court.

Sheikh Hasina’s continued presence in India continues to be a major irritant in relations between the two neighbours. The former prime minister, who fled to India after being ousted in August 2024, has sought a new passport and identity card as she plans to return to Bangladesh in December. But Dhaka has made clear that she can return only if India extradites her. Her proposed return has triggered protests and violence by supporters of her banned party, the Awami League, with bomb blasts and arson attacks reported across at least 28 districts over the past 10 days. Bangladesh has deployed hundreds of paramilitary personnel amid escalating tensions, reports Reuters.

Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi was asked during his visit to Chicago yesterday whether the Congress has considered boycotting elections if it really believes the electoral system is unfair. His answer: “Our strategy is to expose what is going on and take the beating until the people of India realise that the system has been fully demolished.” He told students at the University of Chicago, “If the opposition says we don’t want to contest the election, in the minds of Indian people that process is now illegitimate, and we don’t want it.”

After ‘Go to Pakistan’, it is now ‘Go to Bangladesh’. West Bengal minister Dilip Ghosh on Wednesday defended the killings of people accused of crimes in alleged police gunfights, calling them a “necessary act to decriminalise a criminalised society.” He added that those opposed to the practice should “go to Bangladesh”, offering to facilitate their departure “without a visa”.

Malaysia, meanwhile,...
