Open Tabs: To Resist, or to Collaborate?

Trump says deal-making with Democrats would be “unbelievably productive.” Will progressives take him up on it?

Reid Cherlin

Nov 19

Preview

READ IN APP

Greg Baker/Pool Photo via AP

State of Play: Happy to Help

On Wednesday evening — Thursday morning Shenzhen time — Donald Trump did an interview with Fox News’s Jacqui Heinrich, broadcast live on Laura Ingraham’s primetime show. Presumably the White House agreed to the interview as a way to highlight Trump’s trip to China, and the unprecedented, fairly scary trilateral meeting he was about to step into with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. Fox is in the middle of one of those temporary course corrections where, after an intense period of nonstop shilling for Republicans in an election that didn’t go well, they are playing the skeptic, putting some tougher-than-usual questions to the administration. Heinrich pressed Trump on our relationship with China, on Jensen Huang’s dangerous affair, on the endgame in Iran, on the FAA ground stop. He responded with lots of wacky, novel stuff. But you know what? The election is over, and we no longer have to obsess about all of it. Instead, let’s focus on the one answer making the most waves in political circles.

In the middle of an answer about why Republicans did so badly in the midterms, Trump pivoted, claiming that he’s now getting bombarded with calls from top Democrats wanting to cut deals with him, because he holds the veto power. The exchange went on from there:

Trump: I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years. Because they’ll send me—

Heinrich: You’re talking about Schumer and Jeffries?

Trump: They’ll send me a bill on healthcare. And I’ll say ‘No way.’ And I’ll veto it. And then they’ll call me, and they’ll say— and we’ll sit down. This is what I do in my life, I make—

Heinrich: You’ll have them at the White House soon?

Trump: Sure, I’ll have— I respect them. They won. Politics is a nasty game and they won. And I don’t agree with everything, but I will say this: I think I can do, in many ways, better now.

This is kind of an extraordinary statement, and it’s worth paying attention to. Right now, Congressional Democrats are on war footing, gassed up on their historic 14-point popular vote margin. As we’ll discuss on the show, the focus is on the leadership elections, with progressives trying to replace Schumer and getting Jeffries to commit to early votes on Medicare for All and defunding ICE, and on chest-beating about all the investigations they’re going to launch into Trump’s corruption. In left-leaning online spaces, the general demand is that Democrats give no quarter. Any suggestion that they should instead prioritize finding common ground with Trump is not exactly going to be met with cheers.

Even leaving the ideological battles aside, there’s good reason for skepticism: Trump is all over the place, and it’s a certainty that he’ll be back to defiance and lashing out at “Dumocrats” any moment now. Neither the promotion of Stephen Miller nor the coming blizzard of Congressional subpoenas is going to encourage feelings of charity. Still, if there’s one constant with Trump, it’s Trump’s ego — his hunger to be seen as a great man of history. What the Fox interview shows us is that he can be flattered into being useful. Democrats would be foolish not to take advantage of that. Abdul El-Sayed recognized this when he tweeted an image of a Medicare for All membership card rendered in gold and labeled “Trumpcare” across the top.

“Donald,” he wrote, “this is on the table.”

Coming Attractions

A heads up that for our Sunday episode this week, we’ve got something out of the ordinary: a dispatch from post-election focus groups in Texas and Iowa with Trump voters who went Democratic this time. The project is a collaboration with Future Forward and Orchestra, and it delivered some fascinating insights about the appeal of candidates like James Talarico, Gina Hinojosa, Rob Sand, and Josh Turek, and what swing voters are looking for from Democrats over the next two years. Don’t miss it!

What We’re Watching

Dan’s out today and Tommy’s stepping in, which is great, because we have a bunch of international news to tackle with Trump’s China trip wrapping up. (Of note: White House officials confiscated reporters’ phones when they boarded Air Force One at departure, raising the prospect that he may be making an unannounced stop somewhere — perhaps to meet Kim Jong-Un?) Here’s our plan for news blocks at the moment:

Trump in China: The first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the US, China, and Russia is over — and there’s little to show for it. Trump, Putin and Xi sat around a big, round table. But the show of global power looked more like the gathering of a Potemkin Village council than a committee to rule the world. We’ll ask Tommy for thoughts on whether any of it mattered and then move on to the best sound from the Fox News interview, including Trump’s comments on the Jensen Huang scandal, Iran, and how he characterized his involvement in decisions about spending money on FAA upgrades.

Tech support: Trump continues to insist we have nothing to fear from the rolling outages that sparked turmoil at the FAA, Microsoft, major banks and Apple. What’s his message to anxious Americans? “Tell them to relax. Everything’s good,” Trump told Fox. “I’ll let you know if there’s a problem.” Meanwhile, Playbook reports that DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin is being sidelined by the White House from any more TV appearances after embarrassing, off-message speculation about the cause of the outages and the future of immigration enforcement. Apparently, Stephen Miller personally intervened to shut Mullin down, all the way from Manila. “This is a perfect example of why Stephen was put in the role as chief of staff,” one proud White House official told Playbook. You’d think an effective chief of staff would push the cabinet to provide actual answers, rather than just acting to mute bad ones. But maybe that’s too high a bar for this group.

The Democratic agenda: House Dems rallied behind Hakeem Jeffries, setting him up to become the first Black Speaker of the House in U.S. history and, perhaps, the final Speaker of the Trump era. Jeffries and his allies are girding for battle. Rep. Robert Garcia sent letters to 13 Trump family members and administration officials warning them to save their records. Recipients include Don Jr. and Eric, Stephen Miller, Susie Wiles and JD Vance. This could get feisty.

U.S.-India Insight: Assessing Modi 3.0 Reforms at the Midway Point

U.S.-India Insight: November 2026

View in browser

U.S.-India Insight:

Assessing Modi 3.0 Reforms at the Midway Point

Richard M. Rossow

Senior Adviser and Chair on ​​​​​​India and Emerging Asia Economics

Thursday, November 19, 2026

newsletter14339@gmail.com​​​​​​,

The Modi government is at the midway point of its third term. Contrasted with U.S.-fueled global turmoil, the Indian market has been a beacon of stability. But stability is not the need of the day. Positive change through economic reform is more important than ever, and the track record during this term is mixed, as evidenced by our India Reforms Scorecard. Modi 3.0 is doing well on trade policy and has triggered a few domestic reforms. In its remaining time, the government should also prioritize FDI reforms and push states to improve their business environments.

Power over Policymaking

The Modi government won re-election in 2024 but, with a reduced mandate, was forced into a coalition to retain power. But this position is not a significant detriment to reform; the BJP’s two core coalition partners, the Andhra Pradesh-based Telugu Desam Party (TDP) and Bihar-based Janata Dal-United (JD-U) are not traditionally anti-reform. The BJP continues to strengthen its hand in the upper house of Parliament, the Rajya Sabha. The party holds 117 of 244 seats. And the BJP has its all-time record of 17 chief ministers.

The Crisis that Didn’t Materialize Domestically

A year ago, there was a palpable sense in Delhi that an economic crisis was at hand. The Trump administration was unleashing a trade war with most of the world. India was targeted even more sharply. Crude oil prices had spiked—even before the United States first attacked Iran. This concern drove a few significant reforms in late 2025, notably a rationalization of the Goods and Services Tax; amendments to the Insurance Act; and amending India’s nuclear power development laws.

However, the “crisis” did not really materialize. The government reported 7.8% growth in the first quarter of the fiscal year. FDI inflows have remained relatively strong by Indian standards, hitting $70b from September 2025-October 2026, a 24 percent jump from the prior year. India’s goods exports are up 9 percent year-on-year, and services exports grew 10 percent year-on-year. Foreign portfolio investment (FPI) has been weak with $28b net outflows over 12 months, but India’s SENSEX stock index remains close to record levels.

Domestic Reforms:

The Modi government’s performance this term in pushing big domestic commercial reforms has been mixed. There have been some notable successes such as rationalizing the Goods and Services Tax, liberalizing atomic energy production through the SHANTI Bill, and decriminalizing some types of corporate offenses through the Jan Vishwas Bill. Below the headline reforms, former cabinet secretary Rajiv Gauba has been leading an effort to introduce a range of process reforms at NITI Aayog. These capture fewer headlines but certainly improve the “ease of doing business.”

Other domestic reforms such as privatization, modernizing the Electricity Act, further relaxation of labor regulations, and efficient restitution of business legal cases remains on the “to do list.”

Trade Policy Reforms:

The Modi government’s third term has been most progressive in terms of trade policy. India continues its recent pursuit of tariff-focused trade agreements with key partners. The Union Budget has tended to have more tariff line decreases than increases. And there is a subtle shift away from the use of non-tariff barriers like Quality Control Orders (QCOs).

The government still maintains local manufacturing rules in some sectors. However, this tool has been employed less aggressively this term.

Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) Reforms:

The Modi government has not aggressively pursued additional FDI reforms since early in its first term. Over the last two and a half years, the government has made only a single FDI reform—a legislative change to the Insurance Act that increases the maximum FDI holding in an insurance company from 74 percent to 100 percent.

This record compares unfavorably to the Modi government’s first term (37 FDI reforms in 5 years) and second term (12 FDI reforms) and falls below the average of 20 FDI reforms per 5-year terms under the Vajpayee and Singh governments. Over thirty sectors still have some form of FDI limitation, and at least ten sectors have regulations that only apply to foreign firms.

Encouraging State-Level Reforms:

This is the area of reform that requires the most attention. States control the core factors that will “make or break” India’s economic dreams- electricity, water-sanitation, labor, and land acquisition. Some of the Modi government’s big ideas from its first term, such as creating model policies for states’ consideration and ranking states’ business competitiveness through the Business Reform Action Plan (BRAP) have been discarded and need to be reinvigorated.

Pushing politically challenging economic reforms is challenging when topline data suggests the economy is doing well. However, future coalitions may prove to be more difficult to work with. Future prime ministers may be less business friendly. There will be periods with less center-state political uniformity. And the world is looking for beacons of growth. This could be India’s moment.

​​​​​

Richard M. Rossow

Senior Adviser and Chair in U.S.-India Policy Studies

Richard Rossow is a senior adviser and holds the Chair in U.S.-India Policy Studies at CSIS. In this role he helps frame and shape policies to promote greater business and economic engagement between the two countries. He joined CSIS in 2014, having spent the last 16 years working in a variety of capacities to strengthen the partnership between the United States and India.

Hello. A shocking event occurred on this week in 1987: a fire at a London Underground station which caused 31 people to lose their lives. Below, see how the BBC reported on the tragic incident - and how the safety of the city's famous Tube system was improved as a result. This week's edition of In History also delves into the glitzy wedding of Catherine Zeta-Jones and Michael Douglas 26 years ago. But first, we have extraordinary archive interviews with survivors of the 1978 Jonestown massacre (please note that there are mentions of suicide below).

PS: Just a quick note to say that In History is going to take a break next week due to the public holiday in the US. But we will be back in your inbox on Thursday 3 December. See you then!

VIDEO FROM THE ARCHIVE

How Jim Jones manipulated his followers

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjUsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB3BQFdoWzaGZDP6Mw04B1Q0CEtLbFBGvpyD0HkZ8LMXYAQ7iFiFf_qhASnlXOCN_ziIcddObWKww_1VElo-Ucvsb8J_sSwGobi-uOsM Once courted by the US's political elite, Jim Jones caused the deaths of more than 900 of his followers. Credit: Getty Images

On 18 November 1978, more than 900 people - over 300 of them children - lost their lives after drinking fruit punch laced with cyanide in what became known as the biggest mass suicide in history.

Those who died were followers of US preacher Jim Jones' Peoples Temple church group. "It was mass murder. He completely demolished people's will to live by telling lies," Laura Johnston Kohl, a member of the group who survived the massacre, told the BBC's Witness History in 2015.

At the time of the massacre, Jones and his followers were living in Jonestown, a settlement in Guyana, South America. For many members, this rural commune felt like the Promised Land, far from the problems of the US. For Jones, it provided a way to isolate his followers from their homes and their families.

FIRST DRAFT OF HISTORY

The King's Cross fire of 1987

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjUsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB3BQFdoe8lWUKShW8iI7kAGWbRDzMQuM2ny-KmSy-vFAbhQpbbB00i31O6a5kDkzo5mLfC5QH_CTN1dJU6hbJx8fANfCJ26Dkkm1iLA The aftermath of the fire at London's King's Cross station on 18 November 1987. Credit: Alamy

On this week in 1987, a fire likely caused by a discarded match broke out under a wooden escalator at King's Cross station in central London. It spread rapidly, fuelled by a build-up of grease and dust, and caused the escalator to go up in flames during the end of the evening rush-hour period.

Many passengers were trapped underground, dozens were hurt and 31 people were killed (some instantly and others later, as a result of their injuries).

Around 150 firefighters wearing breathing apparatus spent hours tackling the blaze and helping trapped and injured people reach paramedics on the street above. The fire wasn't brought under control until roughly 9.50pm, more than two hours after it started. One firefighter, Colin Townsley, was killed.

Below, see an original radio script showing how news of the tragic event was shared with BBC radio listeners.

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjUsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB3BQFdofagGRrW-2dJz1_3a_2vVMd-2l9nlCWYe1vxeKItvDjyVeHEHDyre1jWlzj_iNoIYsZW9h78YHlzeceEcz5QBxyKF0gdF3W_g

WHAT HAPPENED NEXT

Changes made to improve safety

No-one was ever prosecuted in connection with the incident, which remains the only mass loss of life in a fire on the London Underground in its 163-year history.

After the fire, huge efforts were made to improve the safety of the London Underground, including rapidly phasing out wooden escalators. The city's Tube system is now considered one of the safest of its kind in the world, managing director Mark Wild told the BBC in 2017, in an article marking 30 years since the King's Cross fire https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjUsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB3BQFdogx3WEUSQONMNyJmQx4xKVGR_uEmKFACMlB3SGg0QVOeTsIsNlre7CFgO8SfQvGy9EGYBULse5J-Iid_3b-cp_f0RdwPzpf3w

"There isn't a month [that] goes by in my job that we don't reference the King's Cross fire," he said. "It had such a phenomenal and beneficial effect on the organisation: so out of a desperate tragedy good things have actually come."

NEWSLETTER · 19 Nov 2026, 18:02

Yalta 2.0? A Putin pipe dream

Also, in tonight’s edition: Health commissioner attacked, hands of Russian assets and European Commission under cyberattack

VIEW IN BROWSER

By Bruno Waterfield

Supported by

Hello, and welcome to Rapporteur PM.

In Shenzhen, the world’s most powerful men met today.

Donald Trump boasted that his talks with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping were “history in the making” with, he said, Ukraine – and therefore Europe – also on the table.

His comments, and the meeting itself, raised the spectre of Yalta, the 1945 superpower agreement that helped cement the Iron Curtain and divided Europe into “spheres of influence”.

Pekka Toveri, a conservative Finnish MEP and retired army general, dismissed the idea as a Russian fantasy, arguing that the real power player is the Chinese president, not Putin or, for that matter, Trump.

“I'm sure that Putin would love to decide Europe's future. But I think the Chinese are in the possible most powerful position,” he said.

Toveri, Finland’s former military intelligence chief, told Rapporteur that Xi knows the US president will leave office in two years and will, most likely, be replaced by a Democratic president, who will not be as close to Putin.

In the meantime, China has little incentive to throw its weight behind a Putin-friendly deal – although that is hardly good news for Europe.

“It's not in their interest to throw themselves into fire for Putin. They are happy with the current situation. As long as the war continues, Russia becomes weaker and weaker and more dependent on China,” he said.

“At the same time, it still splits the West and ties up our resources so that it's more difficult for us to be united against China.”

Toveri also dismissed the idea that the US would agree to Russian demands on the future of European security, such as Moscow’s call for Finland to leave NATO as a condition of peace.

“I totally understand Putin's wish that we wouldn't be there because he conducted the great strategic blunder of pushing us into NATO,” he said, referring to Finland's decision to join the alliance in 2023 in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

“Even if Trump would give the green light to the idea that Finland should leave NATO, nobody else, not even the rest of the US and Europe, would support that."

Supported by Tyres Europe

Tyres are critical to everyday Europe

Ambulances, buses, delivery trucks and tractors all depend on a reliable supply of tyres. An Oxford Economics study shows what EU tyre manufacturing means for Europe’s economy. Learn more here.

Round-up

ASHES TO ASHES: Activists interrupted the EU’s health chief Commissioner, Olivér Várhelyi, as he addressed the European Cancer Summit in Brussels on Thursday, throwing ashes at him in protest against proposed changes to EU pesticide rules.

HANDS OFF: No proposal currently on the table can adequately shield Euroclear and Europe from the legal and financial risks of using frozen Russian assets, a senior executive at Euroclear told MEPs on Thursday. Some €200 billion in Russian sovereign assets are frozen across the EU, most held at the Belgian clearing house.

COMMISSION ATTACK: A European Commission spokesperson confirmed on Thursday that an AI-boosted cyberattack had affected the EU executive’s services since the end of October, but did not confirm whether staff data had been stolen. It also remained unclear whether the attacks were over.

MISMATCH: Europe is leading global efforts to tackle climate super-pollutants, despite an overnight deal in Brussels that will delay new methane emissions reporting requirements by two years, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra has said.

Deep Dives & Analysis

Advancing chip design with OpenAI models (8 minute read)

Design changes proposed by OpenAI's models cut the circuit area of key parts of its Jalapeño AI chip by an estimated 10% to 13%. With AMD, the same approach delivered up to 14% improvements on AMD's flagship GPU designs.

Discuss on TLDR →

Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long? (4 minute read)

In a private benchmark, Gemini 4 Carbon spent close to an hour on bug fixes that Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra finished in minutes. Carbon took about seven times as many steps as Astra, and half were unnecessary.

Switching LLMs mid-conversation is a ski-rental problem (30 minute read)

Most work on routing between language models is centered on making sure the right model handles the right request. A classifier scores the request, then the request is routed to a cheap model if it is easy, and a frontier model if it is hard. For coding agents, this is only half of the problem. The second half of the problem is knowing when a running session should change model. This problem, which this post discusses, has a classic form: the ski-rental problem.

Discuss on TLDR →

Why Antigravity Eats Weekly Quota Fast - and What I Measured (17 minute read)

Google Antigravity wipes users' prompt caches if there is a 5-minute pause. Refreshing the cache just before expiry works, but only for 3 pings. Even a 5-word prompt starts with 13,800 to 16,800+ tokens of system instructions, MCP schemas, and skills. Disabling unused MCP servers and plugins shrinks cold turns and cache misses.

Engineering & Research

Keyboard: 45 wpm. Your voice: 220 wpm. Give Cursor the context it needs (Sponsor)

You can explain a bug out loud in seconds. Typing it out takes long enough that you cut the context, and the answer gets worse. Wispr Flow lets you just talk. It types clean, formatted text into Cursor, Claude or ChatGPT, with the filler words gone. Mac, Windows, iPhone and Android. Try Wispr Flow free

An update on the state of research acceleration at OpenAI (20 minute read)

OpenAI's agents now complete nearly half of two-to-four-hour research tasks on their own. However, humans are still central to AI development. Agent use is surging, and the heaviest users are pulling further ahead. Researchers are devoting increasing human effort to Safety and alignment.

Context API extracts full context from any web page (6 minute read)

The Perplexity Context API can extract the full context from any webpage and return clean Markdown, links, and relevant passages. It can read up to 10 URLs at once. Agents can specify the freshness of each request and validate the source of each result. Every successful result also includes metadata for the page such as the title, description, language, author, and date of publication.

Introducing Model Factory (8 minute read)

Model Factory is a training loop that lets any company train, deploy, and continuously improve models in production. It brings reinforcement learning, supervised fine-tuning, pre-training, and inference together into one control plane. It also offers health checks, automatic node replacement, and recovery from the latest checkpoint for long-running experiments. Model Factory has already been deployed for teams working on finance automation, computer use, scientific discovery, chip design, and other industries.

Miscellaneous

Quickly, There's No Time (38 minute read)

Many things point to the substantial possibility of superintelligence arriving next year. Any plan to prepare for this has to be ready for the full automation of AI R&D, which will result in the rapid advancement of AI abilities beyond human levels. It will need to include mechanisms to slow down the resulting growth in capabilities.

The Silent Consensus (15 minute read)

The most common vision for the future that AI brings isn't totally positive. It is often left unsaid, discernible only by implication, a silent consensus. The decisions humans make will likely lead to a world in which people have forfeited effective authority over much of our civilization. Even if we make extraordinary progress on AI safety and alignment, we could still find ourselves having submitted to a machine entity.

By the way: Our annual Cyber sale is now live—subscribe now and save 50% on an annual subscription. You'll also receive 4 digital research reports focused on AI, energy, and climate tech.

A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for seven weeks, setting a record

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body for seven weeks, smashing the previous record of about two weeks.

They achieved the feat by connecting a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

The approach could open up new possibilities in biomedical engineering, from repairing damaged organs to growing new ones. Some researchers are even exploring artificial wombs.

Take a closer look at the technology keeping human organs alive.

—Antonio Regalado

What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market

After a tough few years littered with high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US: Sila has signed a deal with battery maker Panasonic Energy to supply silicon-carbon anode material that could be worth more than $1 billion.

The agreement will help Sila scale production, potentially bringing smaller, lighter batteries to market. But it also reveals how battery politics have shifted. The factory is backed by a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department—and the industry is increasingly focused on geopolitics rather than the energy transition.

Find out what this deal reveals about the US battery industry.

—Casey Crownhart

New Congress, New Rare Earths Policy?

Congress Should Build Upon, Not Replace, Trump’s Rare Earths Policy

New Congress, New Rare Earths Policy?

+ Wife Insuretech Startup Update and DC Meetup!

Nov 19

READ IN APP

Two announcements before we dive in:

Remember when Jordan’s wife ran a ‘looking for a CTO’ post for an insuretech startup? Well, thanks to the ChinaTalk network, she found an incredible one. They’re now revenue positive and halfway through a seed round. Thank you all for the help!

Jordan will be in DC the week after Thanksgiving for a hot minute and will be hosting a meetup on Dec 2nd.

This piece was authored by anonymous contributor “Matteo Clavijero”.

The blue wave of the midterms has put rare earth companies in the hot seat. Rare earths, particularly those used in the production of permanent magnets, are a critical input enabling trillions of dollars of downstream economic value. Beijing dominates the rare earth magnet supply chain from ore extraction to magnetization, with over 90% of mining, refining, and magnet-making concentrated in China. The CCP has repeatedly sought geopolitical leverage by exercising export restrictions on rare earths to constrict Western economies, and American rare earth competitors have been supported by industrial policy in response. After all, without rare earths the production of a laundry list of technologies — EVs, data centers, drones, wind turbines, smartphones, robots, and more — grinds to a halt.

The US has been attempting to support an ex-China rare earth industry for the past decade, and government support is necessary for any ex-China industry to succeed. Projects are low-margin, decade-long investments that require the government to derisk and backstop ventures, such that the barriers to success are low enough that private investment takes the industry seriously. The second Trump administration has made a flurry of deals, replete with debt financing and equity purchases from the Export-Import Bank (EXIM) and the Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), ostensibly for the purpose of securing America’s critical mineral supply chains.

But many deals have raised eyebrows in the current and incoming Congress, especially deals involving companies with ties to President Trump’s family or his political appointees. In total, the Trump administration has made over a dozen major deals with magnet rare earth operations, with financing packages ranging from just below $100 million to $2.2 billion. Some deals that Congress has targeted include:

USA Rare Earth, a vertically integrated mine-to-magnet company, which received $277 million in federal funding as well as potential access (pending milestones) to a maximum of $1.3 billion in CHIPS loans. In exchange for this financing, the Commerce Department now owns equity in the company. The placement agent for the government deal was Cantor Fitzgerald, a firm formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and currently run by his sons.

Vulcan Elements is making NdFeB magnets in North Carolina, and they received a conditional loan commitment of $620 million from OSC and a $50 million equity deal from Commerce. This deal is under suspicion because 1789 Capital, an investment firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner, invested in Vulcan a few months before the OSC deal. (Trump Jr.’s individual stake in Vulcan is undisclosed, but it seems unlikely that it is higher than 0.5%.1) The OSC deal was allegedly prioritized by Peter Navarro, a White House adviser and personal friend of Trump Jr.

ReElement, a rare earths refining company, which received a $25 million investment from DoW’s Economic Defense Unit (EDU), is under suspicion due to its status as a supply-chain partner of Vulcan.

Energy Fuels, a uranium producer now transitioning to include rare earths capabilities, received a $725 million conditional loan offer from OSC. Energy Fuels’s leaders are currently under investigation by Democratic members of the House for allegedly conducting insider trading before President Trump’s decision to effectively open more areas for Energy Fuels’ processing of uranium and vanadium.

Other deals may be under scrutiny for their equity exchange terms — a preferred tool that is nearly unprecedented in US government policy. The most salient example of this is the landmark MP Materials deal, where DoW purchased $400 million of MP stock and obtained warrants in exchange for a $150 million loan, a ten-year price floor on MP’s NdPr products, and guaranteed offtake of MP Material’s NdFeB magnets. That deal made the Department of War the largest shareholder of MP Materials, the USA’s only currently-operational rare earths mine.

So, what will Congress do about these deals, and what can we expect to happen to the American rare earths push?

The Looming Investigations

Using congressional investigations to discipline the mining industry is not a hypothetical. Besides the House investigation into Energy Fuels, Democratic Congressmen have begun investigating Vulcan, ReElement, and USA Rare Earths. The MP deal remains untouched for now. When the new Congressmen take their seats, we can expect more subpoenas, scrutiny, and Congressional oversight over all of the seemingly unsavory deals.

It is unclear, however, what Congress can actually do about the situation. Many of the aforementioned deals have already been completed; funding has been dispensed, and equity has already been purchased. It will be extremely difficult for Congress to unwind those deals. Future bargains, however, may be unlikely given that due diligence typically requires a year — during which a new appropriation could override the funding authority.

However, many existing deals, particularly EXIM ones, are conditioned on milestones that haven’t yet been met. Companies are still undergoing review processes, holding only Letters of Interest, or pursuing production/technical thresholds necessary to unlock some or all of the money. For such deals, Congress can attempt to withhold appropriations to defund the already-inked contracts, but this is easier said than done. The funding for OSC has already been appropriated by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and EXIM’s charter empowers it to make its own deals. Congress would need to pass legislation to cancel those appropriations and alter the EXIM charter if it wanted to truly neuter the administration’s dealmaking capabilities. And then, of course, any legislation would be subject to a presidential veto.

The only feasible route for walking back some deals is congressional investigation that leads to legal battles. For the companies currently undergoing due diligence for their conditional loans, Congress could unearth evidence of fraud or due diligence violations which may then be referred to the DOJ. The legal mechanism here is still not concrete, but the bad optics could lead to OSC or EXIM unilaterally cancelling deals. The atmosphere at OSC must be pretty awkward right now, and Congress has already begun asking for related offices to keep track of all communication relating to certain deals. Once the Democrats assume the majority, they will no longer be asking but subpoenaing.

Is This the End of the Rare Earths Push?

With some deals in jeopardy, does a Blue Congress spell the death of the rare earths agenda? Likely not, but it does portend a new form of rare earths policy. The Trump administration’s rare earth policy predominantly stemmed from authority in the executive branch — namely in the form of EXIM and OSC reaching agreements with individual companies.

The incoming Congress will likely wrest power away from the executive and instead opt for legislative approaches to critical minerals policy. Instead of officials unilaterally negotiating with companies to give out loans or buy equity, Congressional aspirations would ideally manifest as comprehensive legislation that employs market-wide incentives spanning both the supply- and demand-side to achieve rare earths security.

Several bills along these lines have already been proposed in the current Congress, and we can expect more proposals like these to be brought up in the next session. Promising bills include the Magnets Value Chain Support Act, the National Critical Minerals Council Act, the Critical Materials Future Act, the STRATA Act, the Critical Mineral Executive Coordination Act, and so many more. A sign of encouragement is that all of these bills are bipartisan, so we can hope for a whole-country effort behind these policies.

If Congress can succeed with bipartisan legislation, it can also fail by turning the administration’s deals into a witch hunt. Most of the companies involved in deals don’t deserve to be treated as grift projects; they are often real enterprises in an industry with strategic importance yet meager margins. In the past few years, Congress has offered them no support while the administration has provided badly-needed funding. Throwing them out with the bathwater accomplishes nothing. Even if individually “picking winners” was a suboptimal solution, it was better than no solution at all; Congress must pick up from the state of play and build upon it rather than razing what has already been built.

Upgrade to paid

And an incoming legislative approach is absolutely necessary for the US to achieve rare earth security. Rare earth projects require ten to thirty year time frames to begin exploration, develop and pilot technologies, and then finally scale. Unless investors and companies know that the government is prioritizing these projects for the long haul, the investments will never start to flow, and the projects will never get off the ground.

While the President’s deals were perhaps not to the Democrats’ satisfaction, they spurred the industry to begin moving its wheels. Now, to make sure they keep moving and to attract even more capital, legislation is required to cement incentives regardless of what Party is in control. Whether they be demand-side incentives like the Magnets Value Chain Support Act, tariffs on Chinese magnets, supply-side incentives for firms producing in the US, or whatever else, we need something that lasts. The worst mistake that Congress could make would be cracking down on yesterday’s deals today, while failing to pass anything tomorrow.

Hello. The first ever trilateral talks between the US, China and Russia lasted for 90 minutes - we explain what happened. What should we expect from Anthropic's record-breaking stock market debut? And finally, see how alpacas help students with special educational needs.

Trump leaves China after trilateral talks

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjUsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB3IanBeNVuWh52IbGHq4b-PvlEOw27Cs_9K8yf9S5EyDIUPEvRM-goy8rfkqwmpD7bQw38ji6gWEsxqma4qcXj05SHavSea--nXHf00f Trump said he had a long discussion about the Ukraine war with Putin. Credit: Reuters

President Donald Trump has left the Chinese city of Shenzhen after holding historic talks with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin. A joint statement was issued https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjUsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB3IanBeOWCnkckX1JFm2vXCd8U1vKimb8oz0jJNZ5R7wxVeHIVRdgWQe4Sc1_4msiK_bwQi1-VtM9dDTF2FHgcAwT8i0iNophXt9Xc0p by the three countries afterwards, in which they say "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought". https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjUsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB3IanBei-rx1POXIzc7IJYmF0pecF20ERBwt55KEQprZlIMcjFQ7Ltafg2HQfM6aRQasOwlg2LIfPjAZ_K89_4vucS_5N1sKTSetf3N0 The AI company behind chatbot Claude will be valued at $1.5tn (£1.14tn), having priced its shares at $83. AI giant Anthropic will become one of the most valuable firms in the world after it raised a record-breaking $81bn (£62bn) https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjUsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB3IanBejJ4EIpXiyworr2MopuFm1SkXTNZ48kgdGudhGd5mRl-GC3P0DumeMJhawHMPwDBy1sKNqY3IbB8QTP--P9OJhgJl3fAuo-j-m in its highly anticipated stock market debut. The flotation is being viewed as a test of strength for the AI sector, which faces questions over whether the huge amounts of money being poured into the technology will pay off. Welcome, humans.

So apparently an AI-text detector called Pangram flagged about 99% of a prize-winning Peruvian novel as machine-written, and the publisher kept the prize anyway. The book is Donde el agua trabaja by David Silva Rojas. Mexican publisher Almadía reviewed documents from the author and says it stands by him.

Here's the part that got me. According to El País, Pangram also classified more than 80% of his interview texts and an essay as AI, plus the Instagram post where he denied using AI. Nothing says "I wrote this myself" like a robot-spotter deciding your "I wrote this myself" post was also a robot.

Keep in mind that none of this is verified, and a detector score is an estimate rather than proof. The Authors Guild warns against making one the only basis for a decision. Meanwhile, Gallimard, the French publisher, reportedly plans to start screening manuscripts with Pangram next year.

😸 GAO Says Four Major Chatbots Produced Viable Attack Plans in Covert Tests

The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO), the federal government's watchdog agency, released a report Wednesday saying it got ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok to produce attack plans it judged workable. The tests ran in spring 2026, so they cover the versions available then.

Here's what happened:

GAO picked the four most-used chatbots as of April 2026 and randomly gave each one a scenario, either building and detonating an explosive device or attacking the electrical grid.

Every chatbot's safeguards kicked in at first, with a refusal, removed content, or a suspended account.

GAO says it got past them using common bypass techniques, which the report does not name.

Two chatbots produced explosive plans and two produced plans to attack power substations, all in under 12 hours.

Quick translation. Safeguards are the rules that make a chatbot refuse harmful requests. Bypassing them, often called jailbreaking, means wording a request so the chatbot goes along anyway. Think of talking your way past the bouncer instead of kicking down the door.

GAO counted a plan as viable when it named specific targets, locations, and attack methods, and its experts judged it sufficient to plan and execute an attack. GAO then checked feasibility through research, surveillance, and expert interviews.

Here's the detail worth repeating. GAO says the underlying information was not new. The chatbots gathered what already exists and organized it into a plan fast. Translation: a research assistant that works quickly and never gets tired.

A few caveats. The report labels the chatbots A through D and does not say which one produced which plan. It also does not state the model versions tested, so results may not match today's models. This summary comes from GAO's report page, which lists no recommendations, and the full report runs 61 pages.

Why this matters: Safeguards are what stand between a chatbot and a harmful request, and GAO says common bypass techniques got past them on all four platforms. Company officials told GAO they will keep improving safety, so the thing to watch is whether that holds up when someone repeats this test on current models.

🎓 AI Skill of the Day: Make Your Coding Agent Prove Its Work

The Claude Code team says the way to hand more work to coding agents is to give each agent a way to check itself, so you stop reading every change by hand. Three steps you can borrow from their workflow:

Start with an end-to-end test, which runs a real user flow in the running app, like adding an item to a cart and reaching the confirmation page. When it fails, it shows where the flow broke instead of a vague timeout.

Add a property-based test, which checks a rule that should always hold, like an account balance never going negative, against thousands of generated inputs. Nobody wrote it with the agent's assumptions baked in, so it catches edge cases the agent missed.

If you're replacing old code, run the old and new versions on the same inputs and have the agent chase down any differences, ignoring noise like extra whitespace.

Then set limits. The team lets Claude fix failing checks for up to three rounds before it hands the problem to a human, and the agent never gets to rewrite the rules that judge it. A passing test only proves what it checks, so skim the test too.

Make this change: [describe it]. Before editing, tell me how you will verify [expected behavior]. After the change, run an end-to-end test of that flow plus a test of one rule that should always hold, and report the actual results. If a check fails, fix it up to three times, then stop and tell me. Do not edit the tests to make them pass, and flag anything you could not test.

[AINews] Gemini 4 Neon: GDM's Opus/Sol Contender

November 18, 2026 — Google’s middle tier scores 61 on the Intelligence Index. Plus, Anthropic prices its IPO at $83.

Google DeepMind shipped Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth Gemini 4 model in about seven weeks. If you’re confused about the naming, you’re not alone; the 1.5 month old Argon is now retired, the old Pro and Flash from Gemini 1-3 are dead, and if you’re thinking the names are based on atomic weights, Neon (10), the midtier model is faster/cheaper than Carbon (6). This is a helpful guide to the current leading models and sizes:

Because of how distillation, RL, and benchmarking works, Neon technically outperforms Carbon by some measures despite being a smaller model…

Also today, Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, above its initial range, and Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy Applied Compute in a $4.5B all-stock deal. Anthropic · Palo Alto Networks

AI News for November 17–18, 2026. We checked 12 subreddits and 544 Twitter accounts. Browse past issues.

AI Twitter Recap

Gemini 4 Neon

Launch and availability

Pricing and specs. Neon costs $3 for input, $0.15 for cached input and $15 for output per million tokens. It has a 1M-token context window and four effort levels. Vals reports a maximum output limit of 1M tokens. Google · Vals

Rollout. Neon is coming to the paid Gemini API in AI Studio and Android Studio, Gemini for business, and Antigravity for Pro and Ultra subscribers. In the Gemini app, Pro and Ultra users can select it as “Deeper analysis,” including for Tasks. Google’s rollout · Gemini app

Day-one integrations. Cursor, GitHub Copilot across its app, CLI and VS Code, and LangChain Managed Deep Agents.

Release cadence. Arena counted gaps of 28 days between Argon and Carbon, 15 between Carbon and Hydrogen, and six between Hydrogen and Neon. Arena

Independent results

High versus xhigh. At high effort, Neon matched Carbon’s 60 on the Intelligence Index for $3.74 per task. On GDP.pdf it scored 33.4% at high and 28.0% at xhigh. Artificial Analysis

Agent Arena. Neon debuted second with 1,336 points across about 4,200 sessions. It had a $2.82 median task cost and placed second on steerability. Carbon still leads the separate Text Arena. Agent Arena · Text Arena

Vals. Neon placed second on the Vals Index at 70.9%, about 0.4 points behind Fable 5.2 at less than half the cost per task. On Code Migration it averaged 160 turns, fewer than Carbon’s 234 or Hydrogen’s 574, and scored below both. Vals Index · Code Migration

CursorBench 4.1. Neon scored 63.7% at default effort, up from Hydrogen’s 57.3%. Cursor

Hands-on reports

Steering and capacity. In 13 early Antigravity sessions, Kimmonismus recorded 762 tool calls and a 93% input-cache hit rate. When told to avoid the terminal, Neon ran zero shell commands in those tests. The logs also recorded 57 capacity errors and four stalled runs. Test logs

How teams use it. Theo says he’s now using Neon for copy, Fable to implement changes, and Astra to playtest. Jeremy Howard praised Neon while saying he was reverting Solveit’s Astra and Sol options to their pre-6.2 versions. Theo · Jeremy Howard

New results for GPT-6.2

Math and formal proof. Astra and Sol took the top two spots on MathArena. Astra solved 42 of 53 ArXivLean problems. Vals separately reports what it believes is the first formalization in Lean of Smoktunowicz’s Gap Theorem, with the proof checked by an independent kernel replay. Tim Gehr · Vals

Agent Arena. Astra debuted sixth. Sol placed eleventh at a $0.90 median task cost. On the separate Code Arena WebDev board, Astra placed third at a 42% lower median cost than its predecessor. Agent Arena · WebDev

Background discounts. OpenAI opened a public beta for GPT-6.2 Responses API jobs that can wait. Two-hour and eight-hour targets for the first response come with 30% and 40% discounts per token, respectively. OpenAI Developers

What changed after launch. OpenAI’s Tibo Sottiaux says early reviewers used builds from before the final few days of changes. Artificial Analysis found Astra’s responses got shorter and it was less likely to admit uncertainty in its behavioral evaluation. Sottiaux · Artificial Analysis

Open weights and inference

Correction to yesterday’s Pi adapter numbers. Yesterday’s issue cited 15 to 32 solves on the 51 hardest SWE-bench Pro tasks. Hugging Face reran affected tasks after finding a tunnel outage that hit nine base-model runs. The corrected result is 20 to 33 solves, or 39.2% to 64.7%. It also released an OpenCode adapter that moved Qwen3.8-27B from 35.3% to 51.0% on the same subset with thinking off. Corrected model card · OpenCode release

Tencent releases Hy4 Flash weights. The 224B-parameter multimodal MoE activates 12B parameters per token, supports 1M context and includes a roughly 64B n-gram embedding table. Tencent released instruct, FP8 and base checkpoints. Tencent repository · vLLM

vLLM 0.34.0. The extensible KV cache is on by default and Model Runner V2 is the sole GPU runner. The team reports up to 1.95× faster NVFP4 decoding on GB200. vLLM

Inference capacity grew faster than peak compute. Epoch estimates that the capacity of chips sold for a fixed basket of agent workloads grew 4.6× from Q2 2025 to Q2 2026, while peak 8-bit compute grew 2.6×. Epoch AI

Runway cuts serving hardware in half. It reports serving a 57B video model at 24 fps on four GPUs, down from eight. Runway

Agent tooling. Prime Intellect launched Model Factory for RL, supervised fine-tuning, serving and evals. Hugging Face released the message dataset from its 1,000-agent PyBot project. Prime Intellect · Hugging Face

Research and chip design

OpenAI models help redesign AMD circuits. OpenAI reports up to 14% improvement against optimized baselines on blocks of AMD’s flagship GPU design. The team used Synopsys tools to check that rewritten circuits preserved behavior and to measure power, performance and area. Some changes made it into a design sent for manufacturing. OpenAI

Measuring research acceleration. OpenAI published an update on internal agent use and research task completion, and proposed regular disclosure of indicators for AI research acceleration. OpenAI

Smaller harness edits can save tokens. In a 40-issue held-out test, a gated approach that edited one module at a time scored 40.0% on SWE-bench Lite at 46.7K tokens per task. A full rewrite scored 42.5% at 451.6K tokens. DAIR research summary

Agent teamwork. MAC Bench finds most gains from eight agents came from exploring in parallel. Opus 5.5 was the sole tested model to show an added gain from coordination. Bespoke Labs

Media and voice

Genie 4 reaches Project Genie. Google’s world model adds native audio and lets users change the world with text mid-session. Access is rolling out to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers. Google DeepMind

Turn detection and transcription. Inworld released weights for a voice-isolation model and its SAVA turn detector, which it says detects completed turns in a median 71 ms. AssemblyAI split its 3.7 release into models for voice agents, live transcription and recordings. Inworld · AssemblyAI

Kling Image 4.0. It placed seventh in Artificial Analysis’s text-to-image rankings and sixth in editing. Artificial Analysis

Industry

Anthropic prices its IPO at $83. The offering covers 980M shares, about $81.3B at the offer price. About $79.4B of that comes from shares sold by Anthropic before fees. Nasdaq trading under ANT is expected November 19. Anthropic

Palo Alto Networks agrees to buy Applied Compute. The $4.5B all-stock deal gives Palo Alto a platform for post-training and serving open-weight models. The companies expect to close in Palo Alto’s fiscal Q3 2027, subject to regulatory clearance and other conditions. Palo Alto Networks

AI Reddit Recap

Local audio

Blue TTS v3. A developer says their MIT-licensed model generates audio at about 50× real time on CPU. The thread’s headline number is a throughput claim about that setup. Code and demos · Discussion

Inworld voice isolation. The release includes a 64M-parameter model for offline use and a 58M model for real-time use, both at 48 kHz. Weights · Local tests and discussion

AudioGhost. A local interface for Meta’s SAM-Audio lets users describe a sound in text and separate it from the rest of a recording. Project discussion

Local inference and coding

Experts from an SSD. TokenWing’s developer claims it can stream a majority of routed experts from SSD. A user reported 45–50 tok/s on a 120B MoE with 12 GB of VRAM and 32 GB of RAM. LocalLLM thread

One job, two models. A developer paired GPT-6.2 Astra for planning and review with local Qwen3.8-27B for implementation. The reported API bill fell from $7.40 to $1.62 on that run. Workflow and discussion

Neon’s place in the line-up. Readers discussed whether Neon becomes the everyday replacement for Gemini 3.1 Pro, now that Google has separate tiers for fast work and harder projects. Launch discussion · Tier discussion

When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry. Isabelle Ferreras

When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry. Isabelle Ferreras. We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for Open AI’s product releases said he was quitting the Chat GPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at Open AI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice. Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of Democratic Intelligence.org Continue reading.

Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals a strategy to undercut its AI rivals

Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals a strategy to undercut its AI rivals. Welcome to AI Decoded , Fast Company ‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most important news in the world of AI. I’m Mark Sullivan, a senior writer at Fast Company , covering emerging tech, AI, and tech policy. And if you have comments on this issue and/or ideas for future ones, drop me a line at [email removed], and follow me on X @thesullivan ‘Compute multipliers’ and ‘Anthropic Direct’ may be the IPO’s secret sauce As frontier models from Anthropic, Open AI, and Google converge in capabilities, the companies selling them may end up competing for enterprise business less on model quality and more on the cost of the computing power needed to run them. In its IPO filing and investor roadshow video, Anthropic, which debuted on the Nasdaq on Thursday, suggested it may be preparing for that future with something called “compute multipliers” and a compute-sourcing model it calls Anthropic Direct. In its S-1, filed publicly in October, Anthropic defines compute multipliers as “algorithmic and methodological” improvements in the way it trains and operates models, effectively increasing the computing power it can get from a given amount of capacity. And these multipliers are “stackable.” In its roadshow video , Anthropic says it measures “total effective compute,” which is its physical computing capacity multiplied by the multipliers it has discovered or expects to discover in the future. Its example: If a model takes 100 units of compute to train, a 4x multiplier lets Anthropic train the same model with 25 units, or use all 100 units to train a model that would previously have required 400. The company also says the multipliers “stack,” with each new discovery building on previous ones, and that it expects Claude will eventually be able to discover multipliers on its own. According to the filing, the gains apply to models used to serve customers as well as to model training. Anthropic says its researchers “have delivered meaningful compute multipliers for inference,” reducing the computing power needed to deliver a given level of model performance. The company says this “allows us to provide greater value for customers.” Anthropic has already been cutting prices. It says price reductions tied to new model versions, along with contractual discounts, reduced revenue growth by about $600 million between the second and third quarters of 2026. It says Opus 5.5, launched in September, delivered “a lower cost per task” than earlier models. If Anthropic can get more usable compute out of each chip than its rivals can, it may be able to undercut other AI labs on price. It may also be able to undercut cloud providers that sell AI services built on their own models. If compute multipliers let Anthropic do more with its physical computing power, Anthropic Direct could give the company greater control over where that power comes from. Right now, Anthropic buys almost all it.

As widespread tech outages pile up, AI tools are in the spotlight again

As widespread tech outages pile up, AI tools are in the spotlight again. Inaccessible email inboxes Banking delays And a communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions. In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal. Over the past week alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft , JP Morgan Chase and Apple , and even the U.S. government’s Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency. The Trump administration said there was “zero” indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches. Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages. “To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it’s made them realize how many parts of their lives they’ve handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don’t fully understand,” Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and You Tube, said in an interview. “I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way.” What’s gone offline recently Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors. Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a “latent defect” in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer. For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA’s network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Friday. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights on Monday. Online banking troubles also piled up on Monday. JPMorgan Chase said a software bug affected its internal hardware systems — causing transactional delays for its customers and others sending money to related accounts, sending jitters throughout the financial system before the problem was resolved. And on Tuesday, Apple, Marriott and the NSA joined the growing list. Apple Music, the App Store and Apple Care services were temporarily disrupted after the company said an intern.

What does the Anthropic IPO mean for your 401(k)?

What does the Anthropic IPO mean for your 401(k)?. You may have no interest in investing in AI companies, and you may even suspect that the AI boom is a bubble about to pop But you could already have a stake in one of the industry’s biggest players anyway: Anthropic, which went public today, may be in your retirement account or about to show up there. Some mutual funds, including American Funds Growth Fund of America (AGTHX) and Fidelity Select Technology (FSPTX), hold substantial equity stakes in Anthropic. And some index funds will also soon acquire shares, after recently changing their rules to make it easier for massive companies to join shortly after going public. Previously, companies often had to wait months or a year to be included in major indexes, in part because of concerns about stock volatility. Earlier this year, ahead of the Space X IPO , Nasdaq shortened its waiting period from three months to 15 trading days for qualified mega-IPOs. Nasdaq argued that companies as large as Space X and Anthropic shouldn’t have to wait so long. FTSE Russell has similarly shortened its waiting period to just five trading days, though inclusion depends on how many shares are available for public trading. Morningstar already had a short five-day waiting period, but relaxed its rules about available shares. The S&P 500, meanwhile, still requires companies to wait 12 months and turn a profit before joining—two hurdles Anthropic has yet to clear. When Anthropic is included in a retirement portfolio, it won’t have a large weight initially, Rodney Comegys, chief investment officer at Vanguard Capital Management and head of global equity at Vanguard, tells Fast Company That’s because a relatively small portion of the company’s shares will be available to public investors to begin with. Vanguard has estimated that Anthropic will represent 0.05%–0.15% of its total market index fund. If you have $500,000 in that fund, that might mean $250 to $750 worth of indirect exposure to Anthropic. How to find Anthropic in your 401(k) To know if your 401(k) or an index fund you own will include Anthropic, you’ll have to dig into the details. “Most people don’t look at their index funds, or anything that their 401(k) is invested in,” says John Polonis, a former Wall Street lawyer who now writes about finance. Even if you’ve chosen not to invest in the Nasdaq-100, for example, the stock could still be hiding somewhere else. Other funds, including those that invest in the largest publicly traded companies, could also hold Anthropic shares. “There may be ways that you are getting exposure,” Polonis says, “and if you don’t want any exposure at all, you really have to do a lot of diligence to kind of screen that.” To check your own portfolio, log into your 401(k) account. If you have actively managed mutual funds, look up each fund’s portfolio holdings and search for Anthropic. If you have index funds, check to see which indexes they track.
